messages.subject: Re: [S] making interactions
messages.body_plain:
On Sun, 2 Apr 2000, Ruud H. Koning wrote:

> Hello, I have two variables coded as factors. The first one has
> levels "M" and "F", and the second one has levels "een", "twee",
> "drie", and "vier". How do I create a variable that contains the
> interactions between the two? For example, "M" and "een" should be
> transformed to the new factor level "Meen"?

one <- factor(c("M", "F"), levels=c("M", "F"))
two <- factor(c("een", "twee", "drie", "vier"), levels=c("een", "twee",
"drie", "vier"))
outer(levels(one), levels(two), paste, sep="")

will give you the levels of the combinations. I am not sure what exactly
you want. Suppose I had

v1 <- one[sample(1:2, 20, replace=T)]
v2 <- two[sample(1:4, 20, replace=T)]
nlev <- outer(levels(one), levels(two), paste, sep="")
v3 <- factor(paste(as.character(v1), as.character(v2), sep=""),levels=nlev)
> v1
 [1] M M F F M M F M F F M F M F M F M F F M
> v2
 [1] drie vier een  een  vier een  een  een  een  een  drie een  vier
[14] twee twee drie een  vier drie een 
> v3
 [1] Mdrie Mvier Feen  Feen  Mvier Meen  Feen  Meen  Feen  Feen  Mdrie
[12] Feen  Mvier Ftwee Mtwee Fdrie Meen  Fvier Fdrie Meen 
> levels(v3)
[1] "Meen"  "Feen"  "Mtwee" "Ftwee" "Mdrie" "Fdrie" "Mvier" "Fvier"

might be what you are looking for.

--

messages.subject: [S] Summary - external language question
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Brian Ripley, Henrik Nielsen and Simon Rosenfield for
responding to my somewhat ill posed question about interfacing S-Plus to
another language (one called IDL in this case)

Prof. Ripley pointed out that the easiest method of interfacing S-Plus
with another language is probably to just use file I/O and systems calls
from the S-Plus, if you are using S-Plus to control things (and from
your program in the other language if said language has reasonable
support for system calls). He also mentioned that a more sophisticated
way to approach the problem would be to use DCOM (in Windows and
provided the other language supports DCOM) or CORBA (in Unix) to drive
S-Plus from a program in the other language. He added that another
option would be to interface to RPart provided the other language can
reasonably call compiled C code. He also mentioned that I should be more
careful using the term CART (when I meant to just say classification
using regression trees) as that is a commercial product (and to which I
wasn't referring).

Simon Rosenfield said he had a similar dilemma interfacing S-Plus and
IDL and that it would be sensible to recode things in IDL or just use
file I/O. (And since I used the term CART he  recommended the software
from Salford systems)

Henrik Nielsen graciously sent me an example of some code to interface
S-Plus and C routines.

Thanks again,

-- KY

messages.subject: [S] Summary - Deceptive Graphs
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to David Smith, Marcel Baumgartner, Chuck Taylor, Peter Thyregod,
Marc Kery, John Wildgen, Bert Gunter, Frank Harrell, Jr.,  Joseph Lucke,
Kenton Juhlin, David  Evans, and Douglas McIver who responded to my
question on favorite deceptive graphs. Most responses gave the classic
references on the topic, which are  listed below (Excuse the differerent
formats from cutting and pasting).  I had hoped for less famous examples
such as "the graph on page xx of the Annual Report of the XYZ Company,"
or the paper by John Doe in the current issue of the "Journal of
Whatever Application."

References given:

  Edward R. Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative
        Information, Graphics Press, Cheshire CT, 1983
        (see also his two other books)

        Howard Wainer, Visual Revelations: Graphical Tales
        of Fate and Deception from Napoleon Bonaparte to
        Ross Perot, Copernicus, 1997

        William S. Cleveland, The Elements of Graphing Data,
        Hobart Press, 1985

        William S. Cleveland, Visualizing Data, Hobart Press, 1993

"How to Lie With Statistics", by Darrell Huff, W.W. Norton & Co., New
York,
1954.  ISBN 0 393 09426 X (Paper)

  year = 1984,
  title = {How to display data badly},
  journal = Amer Statistician,

  annote = {graphics; examples of bad graphics}
}

If your notion of graphs includes maps, why not, be sure to look at Mark

Also mentioned was the JASA article on the space shuttle failure: JASA

Several people suggested looking at any issue of USA Today or Time

messages.subject: Re: [S] Bold and Italics
messages.body_plain:
You can try using my "postscriptfonts" package, available from Statlib,
which includes a function mixed.mtext() that allows mixing of fonts using
escape sequences to switch.  Unfortunately, you may not be able to find
and process the font metric files on a Windows system.  You could use the
default font metrics that are packaged with the function, and then by
trial and error figure out the amount of forward or backward space to add
between parts of the label to adjust the approximateness of the default
metrics.  (There is a default to the afm() function that you change to
make this happen.)

messages.subject: [S] RE: [Summary] modeling heterogeneity of Variance
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for all who responded to my question!! It seems there are 3 basic
strategies for dealing with heterogeneity in variance:

a) transform the dependent variable (eg. log(y), or Box-Cox 
   transformation)
b) use weights in the linear regression
c) model the heterogeneity by using gls()

d) modeling this sort of heterogeneity in the random effects of a 
   hierarchical linear model is not yet implemented in the functions
   lme() and nlme()

Here is the copy and paste summary of  the responses, thanks a lot!!!!
Great List!

The question was:
------------------------------------------------------
I am doing a usual linear regression model and discovered by plotting the
predicted values vs. the residuals a strong funnel shape of the
residuals. The residuals are much more heterogenious for lower values of
the covariate than for higher values.

Can anyone give me a hint how to incorporate that into the analysis - what
functions do I use? How would I have to change the lm()-statement?

fit<-lm(AV ~ COV, data=blabla)

I have the same situation in a Hierarchical Linear Model, where the
level-2 residuals (random effects) have a similar shape if they are
plotted vs. a level-2 covariate - is there a way to handle that in this
more complicated situation?     
------------------------------------------------------

The responses were:
------------------------------------------
Ed Malthouse:         
Could you apply a variance stabilizing transformation to the
dependent variable, e.g., log or square root?

fit<-lm(log(AV) ~ COV, data=blabla)

------------------------------------------

----------------------------------------- 
Paul Lin:  

When you have heteroscadasticity as such, you will need to first perform
some variance stablizing transformation such as the Box-Cox transformation
of the dependent variable.  Then the linear regression performed on the
transformed data will then better satisfy the usual regression
assumptions.

I have never perform a Box-Cox transformation in Splus, so I couldn't
advise you on the exact code.  But it shouldn't be too hard to find out
via the help system. 
-----------------------------------------

-----------------------------------------
Peter Ellis:

You have several options.  You could choose to model the variance ie maybe
estimate its relationship to COV (there are a variety of ways to do this,
depending on how your data is), and then use the "weights" option in lm to
set weights equal to the inverse of the estimated variance.  
Alternatively, maybe try a transformation.  Sometimes modelling log(AV) on
log(COV) will keep a fairly linear relationship and get rid of the
heteroscedasticity.  Obviously, try plotting the transformed data first.  
You may lose the linearity, or maybe you have some other (eg
non-statistical, or interpretation) reason for not wanting to transform.  
-----------------------------------------

-----------------------------------------
Jose' Pinheiro:
It sounds like you should be using weighted least squares to account
for the heteroscedasticity in your data. The lm function takes an
argument, weights, for that kind of fit. Assuming, from your
description, that the variance decreases according to 1/COV, you can
use

  fit <- lm(AV ~ COV, data = blabla, weights = COV)

If you need more flexibility in the choice of weights (e.g., you may
want to use var(y) = COV^theta, where theta is a parameter to be
estimated from the data), you may want to use the gls function in the
NLME library (available from http://nlme.stat.wisc.edu and included
with S-PLUS 2000 for Windows).                         

The lme function in the NLME library allows you to specify variance
functions to account for heteroscedasticity in the within-group
errors, but, at this time, it does not allow variance functions for
the random effects. Certainly a worthwhile feature to be included, but
still in the "to do" list.        
-----------------------------------------

-----------------------------------------
Nick Ellis

Sounds like you might need to transform the data with a power law. You
could try the boxcox() function in V&R's MASS library. This will give you
an estimate of the power to use, and confidence intervals.
-----------------------------------------

----------------------------------------
Matthias Richard (doctoral candidate)

Center for Research on Psychotherapy
Christian-Belser-Str. 79a
70593 Suttgart
Germany

telephone: ++49-711-6781-408
http://www.psyres-stuttgart.de

messages.subject: [S] Robust ANOVA
messages.body_plain:
Another approach to robustification is to use a rank-based analysis such as the 
proportional odds model (the lrm function in the Design library will do this, 
for example).  The PO model generalizes Wilcoxon-Kruskal-Wallis type tests to 
continuous variables and covariable adjustment.  A somewhat well-kept secret is 
that you can have one intercept per unique value of Y (less one reference 
category) without causing statistical or numerical problems (other than an 
increase in run time).  So you don't have to categorize Y to use the PO model.

--
Frank E Harrell Jr
Professor of Biostatistics and Statistics
Division of Biostatistics and Epidemiology
Department of Health Evaluation Sciences
University of Virginia School of Medicine
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

messages.subject: [S] Transforming Y
messages.body_plain:
Besides Box-Cox transformations another possibility is Tibshirani's AVAS 
algorithm which uses Friedman's "super smoother" to solve for a transformation 
of Y that stabilizes variances.  I have packaged the S-Plus avas() function in 
the Hmisc library's areg.boot function, which provides bootstrap confidence 
intervals for a variety of quantities from the model including confidence bands 
for the transformations of all the variables.  areg.boot also can use Duan's 
smearing estimator to get predicted mean(Y) on the original scale.  For an 
example see the last talk listed under 
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/presentations/index.html, or see 
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s/help/transace.html for documentation 
to areg.boot.  areg.boot takes into account the uncertainty in the Y-transform 
when computing all confidence intervals.  Failure to take into account this 
uncertainty can result in falsely narrow intervals.

--
Frank E Harrell Jr
Professor of Biostatistics and Statistics
Division of Biostatistics and Epidemiology
Department of Health Evaluation Sciences
University of Virginia School of Medicine
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

messages.subject: [S] Bold and Italics Revisited
messages.body_plain:
All:

Thanks to Alan Zaslavsky and Bert Gunter for their responses to my question
about bold and italic font settings in S-Plus 2000 for a windows 95
operating system (their responses can be seen below).  The quick answer is
that it can NOT be done easily in S-Plus.  

George Bagnall
gbagnall at cadmusgroup.com

Alan Zaslavsky:
You can try using my "postscriptfonts" package, available from Statlib,
which includes a function mixed.mtext() that allows mixing of fonts using
escape sequences to switch.  Unfortunately, you may not be able to find
and process the font metric files on a Windows system.  You could use the
default font metrics that are packaged with the function, and then by
trial and error figure out the amount of forward or backward space to add
between parts of the label to adjust the approximateness of the default
metrics.  (There is a default to the afm() function that you change to
make this happen.)

Bert Gunter
In other words, Alan, it really can't be done ;-) .

Seriously, suppose we want to produce a standard .wmf file with such text.
One possibility is to use separate mtext calls to overwrite the different
fonts, fiddling with spacing so it looks halfway decent. But that's pretty
dumb, I think. Generally speaking, in the Windows environment, the way to do
it is NOT to do it: If you really want fancy annotation, import the graph
into Word or Excel or whatever and use their annotation tools to write on
the image. Again, most inelegant and unreliable, but it may be the best
among poor choices.

Cheers,

Bert Gunter

messages.subject: [S] Statistical Reports with S+ and SAS
messages.subject_clean: [S] Statistical Reports with S+ and SAS
messages.body_plain:
I sent this note about a week ago but it was intercepted from being posted to 
s-news because it contained html.  Here is a plain text version.  I'm hoping in 
the future that the s-news postmaster will decide to allow html.  -Frank

P.S. I am currently updating the comparison between S-Plus and SAS we have in 
the online document listed below.  SAS has made several changes in Version 8.  
Thanks to Doc Muhlbaier for reminding me to work on this.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 
To add to what Bill Pikounis said so well, one thing that should make
statisticians more comfortable with using S-Plus for FDA submissions is the
fact that many statisticians at FDA use S-Plus.  Here are some other
thoughts.

  1. If you want to couple S-Plus to LaTeX as we and the University of
Wisconsin have done you can have superior statistical reports.  It's also
easy to generate hyperlinked pdf documents containing the report.  FDA
likes pdf format.  See
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s/LiveDoc.html for more
information.
  2. For some of the reporting functions in the Hmisc library for making
tables there are corresponding plot methods for converting the same table
to a graphic (just as there is a latex function for converting the table to
LaTeX, using different font sizes for different table elements if needed).  
I have found this to be a very effective use of object-oriented
code.
  3. I have not had SAS on my machine in 4 years, and haven't missed it
  4. Once you get comfortable with the S language you will find that
manipulating and recoding data is better in  S-Plus than in SAS (see
Chapter 4 in http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s/doc/splus.pdf).  One
example of this is recoding from one variable to a character variable
having many levels by treating the levels as a  vector instead of using
several IF statements.
  5. S-Plus is better for table making than SAS

I know a lot of statisticians will argue with the last two points
especially - most people think that SAS is at its best in making tables.  I
have found that the reverse is true.  With S-Plus and especially when
coupled with LaTeX I can make very nice tables with minimal programming,
whereas with SAS special macros need to be used to produce the different
output for categorical (e.g., percentages) vs. continuous (e.g., quantiles)
variables.  In S-Plus a function can sense what type of data are being
analyzed (e.g, numeric, character, categorical, binary, multiple choice,
numeric with only 5 unique values, etc.) and do the appropriate summary.
Regarding complex data recoding, I can do this better using S-Plus functions
than using SAS statements and macros.  Terry Therneau rightfully argues that
a disadvantage of this approach is that it is more difficult for others to
read such S-Plus code than to read several SAS IF statments.

-Frank Harrell

messages.body_plain:
One possibility worthy of research into its performance is Tibshirani's 
"bootstrap bumping" procedure in which you choose, of say 100 bootstrap fits, 
the "best" of those fits that satisifies the constraint.  See 
http://www-stat.stanford.edu/~tibs/research.html under his 1995 papers.  
bumping is facilitated by the Design library's bootcov function but you would 
need to add a little bit of code of your own.

One side benefit of "bumping" is that it provides a "poor persons Bayesian 
posterior probability" that the constraint is satisfied in the population, by 
computing the proportion of bootstrap samples satisfying the constraint.  
-Frank Harrell

According to Rolf Turner:
|>

|> Let me add a fervent amen to A.J. Rossini's recent posting on HTML in
|> email.  It's a right pain.

I know many people whose lives are occupied with a range of subtleties
other than the difference between character, date, integer and all the
rest of them.  Some people want to send a letter and paste a picture
into it, just like they used to send to their grandma.  Now they want
to do that via computer.  And that's fair enough.

The problem with HTML is not that it can be sent.  Rather, it's not
obvious how to switch it off.  I receive email from people much older
and much younger than myself who just can't work out how to keep it as
plain text.  I like to use a simple mailer such as elm which can do
everything from the keyboard far more quickly than anything I've seen
which uses a mouse.  That is until someone sends me HTML.

|> a web browser for web-browsing.  They should be separate entities;
|> otherwise they tend to create a mess and cause confusion.  cheers,

It's not all that hard to deal with, though.  I bounce such mail to a
Yahoo! address and paste the text into an emacs buffer (from the
dreaded Netscape).  Simpler than trying to direct someone through
menus I can't see.

However, for posters to Snews, I do not think it an outrageous
expectation that they be able to work out how to switch off HTML.

messages.subject: [S] Help: Memory usage
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users

I need your help using scripts in S-Plus.
I am running S-Plus 2000 on Win NT 4.01 with PIII-733 MHz and 1 GB RAM

When I select the following script for over night runs, S-Plus runs out of
memory:
# 1. calculation
        df <- read.table(large table)

        tmp <- function(df)

        final.1 <- function(tmp)
        write.table(final.1)

# 2. calculation
        df <- read.table(large table)

        tmp <- function(df)

        final.2 <- function(tmp)
        write.table(final.2)
# 3. claculation
etc.

Because of out-of-memory error, I lost the final data, since S-Plus did not 
store them in the working directory immediately.
To avoid this I added synchronize():

# 1. calculation
        df <- read.table(large table)

        tmp <- function(df)

        final.1 <- function(tmp)
        synchronize()
        write.table(final.1)
# 2. claculation
etc.

Sorrowly, this does not prevent S-Plus from increasing memory usage
with every calculation. 
I tried to remove also the temporary files with rm(..):

# 1. calculation
        df <- read.table(large table)

        tmp <- function(df)

        final.1 <- function(tmp)
        synchronize()
        write.table(final.1)
        rm(df,tmp)
# 2. claculation
etc.

Sorrowly, this did also not have any effect on memory usage.
I used a test script and watched the task-manager from NT.
Whatever I tried, the MEM usage increases with every calculation step,
even when using the same name for the temporary files (df, tmp).

Is there a command which I can add in the script, which frees memory??

Thank you in advance
Christian Stratowa

Multiple Comparisons and Multiple Tests Peter Westfall  This session will
review multiple 
comparisons and multiple testing methods, from basic to advanced, from a
perspective applied 
statisticians including those in pharmaceutical and regulatory environments.
Philosophical issues of 
"family" choice, combined versus component tests, interval versus test-based
inference, Intersection-
Union versus Union-Intersection tests, False Discovery Rate versus
Familywise Error Rate, and 
Bayes/frequentist views will be discussed.  The emphasis will be on closed
testing procedures, interval-
based inference, and power analysis;  with specific presentation of Holm,
Hochberg, Hommel, Rom, 
Shaffer, Westfall-Young, Tukey, Dunnett, Hsu, Edwards and Berry, Lehmacher,
fixed sequence and 
gatekeeping methods.  Applications include comparisons (all pairs, versus
control, or general directed)
the ANOVA, ANCOVA, MANCOVA (with solutions for heteroscedasticity), tight
confidence bands,
general mixed models, binary data and discrete data models (exact and
asymptotic). Case studies
include ranking of treatments, multiple endpoints in clinical trials,
subgroup analysis, dose response 
analysis, multiple time point analysis, genetic associations, and adverse
events.  
Textbook recommended: Multiple Comparisons and Multiple Tests Using the SAS®
System,
 by Westfall, Tobias, Rom, Wolfinger, and Hochberg (SAS Books by Users
Series, June 1999)?.  
 ? This book will be available to participants at a discount. Call (215)
591-9010 for details

Exact Inference for Categorical and Nonparametric Data Cyrus R. Mehta  Exact
methods of
inference are based on permuting the observed data in all possible ways so
as to derive exact 
distributions for the test statistics of interest, and thereby compute exact
p-values and exact confidence 
intervals. These methods require no large-sample or distributional
assumptions for their validity. They 
produce reliable inferences in small or large samples, balanced or
unbalanced datasets, normal or 
non-normal data, and  contingency tables with zero cell counts, small cell
counts or a mixture of zero, 
small and large cell counts. A familiar example is Fisher's exact test for a
2x2 contigency table. 
These methods can, however, be applied to most commonly encountered
statistical problems including 
one-, two- and K-sample tests, ordered and unordered RxC contingency tables,

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I use S+2000.

I have data that are analogous to the Pixel 
example described in the S+ statistics manual. 
In the example, the dependent variable "pixel" 
is the mean value of intensity measurements in 
the right and left lymph nodes of dogs. Suppose 
that I would like to include the (at presumably 
random locations) individual measurements which 
in my case are unbalanced (i.e. not the same 
number of observations on each side in each 
dog). I guess my first action is:

pix <- groupedData(pixel ~ day | dog / side / 
sub-side, data =    Pixel) 

Question 1: what would be the plot statement?

Question 2: how do I arrange my data?

Something like?

dog  side   sub-side   pixel         day
 1      L        L1           .1      1
 1      L        L1           .1      2
 1      L        L1           .1      3
 1      L        L2           .3      . (point = 
several days)
 1      R        R1           .1       .
 2      L        L1           .2      .
 2      R        R1           .4       .
 2      R        R2           .5       .
 2      R        R3           .7       .
 3    etc (N.B. R1 in dog 1 and R1 in dog 2 etc. 
have nothing in common except that they were 
located somewhere in the right lymph node)

Question 3: do I need to include "sub-side" in 
the fit model, or is that automatically done?

Suppose that the right side got a treatment and 
the left side served as control, would the 
following model be legitimate?

pixel.fit <- lme (fixed = pixel ~ day * side, 
data = Pixel, random = dog ~ day)

messages.subject: [S] GLiM with proportion data
messages.body_plain:
Dear all

I am  a real bigginer in using S+2000/windows95, and I apologise for the 
"stupid" question. I want to make a GLiM regression in order to explain a 
proportion variable by different kind of explainatory variables 
(categorical and continuous). I do not really know the exact procedure.

I have tried several where:

PropLt is the proportion to explain (proportion of succesful infective 
larvae of a parasite)

ExpLt is a kind of experiment (categorical with 4 modalities)

ILt is the infectious dose (initial number of larvae)(continuous)

A)
bin1<-glm(formula = PropLt ~ ExpLt + ILt, family
+        = binomial(link = logit), data =
+       TotLeigh, na.action = na.exclude,
+       control = list(epsilon = 0.0001,
+       maxit = 50, trace = F))

> anova(bin1, test="F") (* Chi provides absurd results *)

or

B)
> bin2<-glm(formula = PropLt ~ ExpLt + ILt, family
+        = binomial(link = logit), data =
+       TotLeigh, weights = ILt, na.action
+        = na.exclude, control = list(
+       epsilon = 0.0001, maxit = 50,
+       trace = F))

> anova(bin2, test="Chi")

or

C)
> binq<-glm(formula = PropLt ~ ExpLt + ILt, family
+        = quasi(link = logit, variance =
+       "mu(1-mu)"), data = TotLeigh,
+       weights = ILt, na.action =
+       na.exclude, control = list(epsilon
+        = 0.0001, maxit = 50, trace = F))

> anova(binq, test="F")

All give similar results except B) where P values =0 (too low for the 
quality of data I think)

And they are similar to a GLiM with gaussian error and a Arcsin(sqrt) 
transformation of the variable to explain.

Which is the best if any? If none what should be done?

Thank you very much

Sincerely

Thierry

messages.subject: [S] predictions using lme() with AR(1) serial correlation and variance heteroscedasticity
messages.subject_clean: [S] predictions using lme() with AR(1) serial correlation and variance heteroscedasticity
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

A few days ago, a question was asked to S-news on how to compute
predicted values given an AR(1) correlation structure for residuals (see
below). How can I compute predicted values when I have both an AR(1)
serial correlation, and variance heteroscedasticity for residuals. In my
actual data, variance heteroscedasticity was modelled with varPower()
function.

Many thanks in advance and best regards,

Renaud

"COOPER, Andy" wrote:
> 
> I would like to thank Jose Pinheiro and James Roger for their wonderful help
> on this!!  Here's a summary (actually, it's a cutting and pasting) of their
> replies.  I hope that in my cutting and pasting that I have not
> misrepresented any of what was said.
> 
> Thanks again for everyone's help!!
> 
> -- Andy
> 
> The current version of the NLME library, 3.2, does
> not produce predictions that take into account the correlation
> structure of the within-group errors, when an individual has been
> previously observed. This is a topic in the "to do" list that will
> eventually be incorporated into the code, but not into the immediate
> future.
> 
> > My question is how does Phi get incorporated into a predictive equation?
> > I've looked in the standard Splus sources and wasn't able to find an
> answer.
> >
> > My intuition tells me that I'd simply use an equation like:
> >
> > yhat(t) = b0hat + b1hat*x1(t) + b2hat*x2(t) + b3hat*x1(t)*x2(t) + BLUP(i)
> -
> > 0.691*yhat(t-1)
> >
> > Where "t" indexes the time (which is discrete).  Am I thinking of this
> > correctly?
> 
> Almost. The correlation structure applies to the within-group errors
> and only indirectly to the responses, y_t. In the case of corAR1, the
> model is
> 
>         e_t = phi * e_{t-1} + u_t
> 
> where the u_t are iid N(0, sig2). The prediction for a previously
> observed individual has two components: one associated with the fixed
> and random effects (what's currently returned by the predict function)
> plus a prediction for the within-group error. The formula in your case
> would be
> 
> yhat(t) = b0hat + b1hat*x1(t) + b2hat*x2(t) + b3hat*x1(t)*x2(t) + BLUP(i) -
>     0.691*ehat(t-1)
> 
> where ehat(t-1) is the within-group residual at time t-1, given by
> 
>  y(t-1) - (b0hat + b1hat*x1(t-1) + b2hat*x2(t-1) +
>         b3hat*x1(t-1)*x2(t-1) + BLUP(i))
> 
> Note that ehat(t) can only be calculated as above for the observed
> t. For forecasting, you could use ehat(t+1) = phi * ehat(t),
> ehat(t+2) = phi^2 * ehat(t), and so on.
> 
> Thus, for pointwise predictions for individuals not previously observed, the
> Phi does not come into play (nor do the BLUPs). The idea behind the
> predictions is that you are trying to get the conditional expectation of the
> unobserved response given the observed data. If the new observation is
> independent of the observed data, the best you can do is to use the marginal
> expectation, which only depends on the fixed effects. However, the phi is
> used in the derivation of prediction intervals for the new value (though we
> have not yet implemented it in NLME), so it's important to get its
> estimate.
> -----------------------------------------------------------------------

messages.subject: Re: [S] GLiM with proportion data
messages.body_plain:
> 
> Dear all
> 
> I am  a real beginner in using S+2000/windows95, and I apologise for the 
> "stupid" question.  I want to make a GLiM regression in order to explain a 
> proportion variable by different kind of explainatory variables 
> (categorical and continuous). I do not really know the exact procedure.
> 
> I have tried several where:
> PropLt is the proportion to explain (proportion of succesful infective 
> larvae of a parasite)
> ExpLt is a kind of experiment (categorical with 4 modalities)
> ILt is the infectious dose (initial number of larvae)(continuous)
> 
> A)
> bin1 <- glm(formula = PropLt ~ ExpLt + ILt, family
> +      = binomial(link = logit), data =
> +     TotLeigh, na.action = na.exclude,
> +     control = list(epsilon = 0.0001,
> +     maxit = 50, trace = F))
> 
>  > anova(bin1, test="F") (* Chi provides absurd results *)

Chi provides absurd results because you have not declared a
weight argument and it is treating the data as it would binary
data (even though it is not 0-1).  Is there a good reason for
having this initial number as a predictor?  I find it a bit odd.

> 
> or
> 
> B)
>  > bin2<-glm(formula = PropLt ~ ExpLt + ILt, family
> +      = binomial(link = logit), data =
> +     TotLeigh, weights = ILt, na.action
> +      = na.exclude, control = list(
> +     epsilon = 0.0001, maxit = 50,
> +     trace = F))
> 
>  > anova(bin2, test="Chi")
> 

You say the initial number of larvae is continuous, is this
because there is a very large number and you do it by weight (or
volume) rather than by counting?  If so your larva by larva
outcomes are unlikely to be truly independent and you proportions
will most likely behave like binomial proportions, at least not
with ILt as the effective number of trials (even if you do a
conversion from weights to approximate true numbers).

> or
> 
> C)
>  > binq <- glm(formula = PropLt ~ ExpLt + ILt, family
> +      = quasi(link = logit, variance =
> +     "mu(1-mu)"), data = TotLeigh,
> +     weights = ILt, na.action =
> +     na.exclude, control = list(epsilon
> +      = 0.0001, maxit = 50, trace = F))
> 
>  > anova(binq, test="F")
> 

This is close to what, in the absence of more complete
information, I would suggest as a first try.  It amounts to
saying the behaviour of the proportions is *like* binomial
proportions but you only know the effective numbers of trials up
to a constant of proportionality (effectively your estimated
scale parameter).

Again, I am puzzled about having ILt in as a predictor as well as
a weight variable.  It's provisionally reasonable, but in my
experience unusual.  It does rather emphasize that would not
really expect the sort of independence you would need for true
binomial proportion behaviour, though.  

I would expect the estimates of parameters to be very similar
under all three schemes, but the standard errors and deviances
would probably be quite different.

> All give similar results except B) where P values =0 (too low for the 
> quality of data I think)

> And they are similar to a GLiM with gaussian error and a Arcsin(sqrt) 
> transformation of the variable to explain.

Yep.  This might be a safe sort of course, but you should use ILt
as a weight variable even in this case.

> 
> Which is the best if any? If none what should be done?

It sounds to me as if you need to consult a professional
statistician.  It takes more than a good software package to get
this stuff right, you know....

> Thank you very much
> 
> Sincerely
> 
> Thierry

--

messages.subject: [S] Summary of Unique rows in a dataframe
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary of Unique rows in a dataframe
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for all the great help on this problem.  Below is my original
questions followed by a quick summary of answers.

I ended up using Bill Dunlap's agg.length() function.  It worked like a
charm even with a data frame with 4 columns and 200,000 observations.

Thanks also to Renaud Lancelot who pointed out that I could search for
questions to potential FAQ at:

http://www.biostat.wustl.edu/s-news/s-news-archive/search.html

Paul Bliese
Walter Reed Army Institute of Research

ORIGINAL QUESTION:
I have a data frame with 11 rows and 3 columns.  Three of the rows have the
exact same data.  I would like to get rid of these duplicates and return a
dataframe containing only the 8 unique rows.

Example:
> TDAT
   T1 T2       T3 
 1  A  1 11/15/99
 2  A  1 11/29/99
 3  A  2 11/15/99
 4  A  3 11/15/99
 5  B  1 11/15/99
 6  B  1 11/15/99 *
 7  B  1 11/15/99 *
 8  B  3 11/15/99
 9  C  2 11/15/99
10  C  2 11/15/99 *
11  C  3 11/15/99

*=duplicated

I can use aggregate.data.frame and it works fine for my example. 

aggregate.data.frame(TDAT[,1],TDAT,length)
  T1 T2       T3 x 
1  A  1 11/15/99 1
2  B  1 11/15/99 3
3  A  2 11/15/99 1
4  C  2 11/15/99 2
5  A  3 11/15/99 1
6  B  3 11/15/99 1
7  C  3 11/15/99 1
8  A  1 11/29/99 1

I haven't been as successful using the aggregate.data.frame solution with a
very large dataframe (>200,000 rows).  Is there a more elegant (and more
efficient)solution?

ANSWERS:

1. Peter Perkins

duplicated2 <- function(x)
{
        #
        # find duplicate rows of a matrix or data frame
        #
        pmat <- do.call("paste", as.data.frame(x))
        duplicated(pmat)
}

2. Carlisle Thacker

TDAT[!duplicated(paste(
        as.character(TDAT$T1),
        as.character(TDAT$T2),
        as.character(TDAT$T3))),]

3.  Bill Dunlap

You could use the following, agg.length(by), which does the equivalent of
aggregate(x, by, FUN=length).  It avoids splitting the dataset
into lots of tiny pieces and calling length on each one.  It returns the
data in a different order than aggregate (sorted by each of the by columns).
Use sort.it=F only if you know your data is already sorted appropriately
or if time is implicitly used in the aggregation.

agg.length <- function(by, sort.it = T) {
        if(!is.data.frame(by))
                by <- data.frame(by)
        if(sort.it) {
                ord <- do.call("order", by)
                by <- by[ord,  ]
        }
        logical.diff <- function(group)
        group[-1] != group[ - length(group)]
        change <- logical.diff(by[[1]])
        for(i in seq(along = by)[-1])
                change <- change | logical.diff(by[[i]])
        by <- by[c(T, change),  , drop = F]
        by$length <- diff(c(0, seq(len = length(change) + 1)[c(change, T)]))
        by
}

messages.body_plain:
Perhaps I can ask for help with a question somewhat similar to my earlier one.

The important part of a function definition (line numbers added here only) is--

1 "get.bwplot" <- function(in.var)
2    {
3    # Make the actual plot:
4    Fred <- bwplot(cv.err  ~ in.var | alpha * m, data=all.e)
5    }

When called with

   get.bwplot(e.msy)

(where e.msy is a column of data.frame all.e)

this fails with an error like "Object in.var not found."  However, if 
"in.var" on line 4 is replaced with (not in quotes) "e.msy", the call succeeds.

Clearly, I do not understand calling conventions in this language.  Is this 
usage a problem because in this case the argument is only one *column* of a 
data frame, rather than an object per se defined in the calling frame?  But 
why would that be a problem, given "lazy evaluation" and the fact that data 
frame itself is apparently recognized in the same statement?

Is there a principle here I don't understand, and how can I observe it?

...Mike Prager

> Clearly, I do not understand calling conventions in this language.  Is this 
> usage a problem because in this case the argument is only one *column* of a 
> data frame, rather than an object per se defined in the calling frame?  But 
> why would that be a problem, given "lazy evaluation" and the fact that data 
> frame itself is apparently recognized in the same statement?
>

Look up the S scope rules.  in.var is in the frame of get.bwplot, and so is
not visible from inside functions called from get.bwplot, like bwplot,
unless the authors of the called function have worked around this.
You need to assign in.var in frame 1 to make it visible.

Incidentally, bwplot does not plot the data: print.trellis does. I have
never been sure if creating a trellis object and printing it in another
frame always finds the data: I know it should!

messages.subject: Re: [S] Column names as arguments
messages.body_plain:
"Mike Prager" <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov> writes:

> Perhaps I can ask for help with a question somewhat similar to my earlier one.
> 
> The important part of a function definition (line numbers added here only) 
> is--
> 
> 1 "get.bwplot" <- function(in.var)
> 2    {
> 3    # Make the actual plot:
> 4    Fred <- bwplot(cv.err  ~ in.var | alpha * m, data=all.e)
> 5    }
> 
> When called with
> 
>     get.bwplot(e.msy)
> 
> (where e.msy is a column of data.frame all.e)
> 
> this fails with an error like "Object in.var not found."  However, if 
> "in.var" on line 4 is replaced with (not in quotes) "e.msy", the call 
> succeeds.

> Clearly, I do not understand calling conventions in this language.  Is this 
> usage a problem because in this case the argument is only one *column* of a 
> data frame, rather than an object per se defined in the calling frame?  But 
> why would that be a problem, given "lazy evaluation" and the fact that data 
> frame itself is apparently recognized in the same statement?

It's not the calling conventions - it's the "scoping" of variables.
If you can get a copy of Venables and Ripley (1997) (i.e. the second
edition), read section 4.8 on Frames and especially the warning at the
top of page 154.  In short, functions called from within another
function do not have access to the objects defined in the caller.
They do have access to the objects defined globally.

(The reason that you need V&R 2 is that this material was omitted from
the 3rd edition because it is covered in the soon-to-be-released
companion volume "S Programming".  If you can't get a copy of V&R 2
then wait for "S Programming" to be published in the very near future.
That covers these types of issues in much greater detail.)

There is a work-around and that is to store a copy of in.var in frame
1.  See the documentation for the "assign" function.

Note that you probably don't want to define your get.bwplot function
so the last operation is an assignment.  Also, be careful that bwplot
(and all other Trellis functions) does not draw a plot.  It produces a
trellis object that draws a plot when it is printed.

messages.subject: [S] Periodic Splines and Gams
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

   I have some disease incidence data that was collected over several,
non-contiguous complete years. I am interested in looking at how the
incidence rates change over a year by using month as an explanatory
variable.  

   I am going to model this using a gam with 
      i)   events as the response and  
      ii)  population at risk as an offset 
      iii) a Poisson distribution and log link with
      iv)  (smoothed) month and (unsmoothed) age (2 levels),  sex(2 levels)
and year as explanatory factors.

   My problem is that I'd like to be able to smooth month under the
condition that January follows December i.e. they are 1 month apart and not
12 months apart. (If I didn't have to take account of the other factors
then I could just use spline(x,y,periodic=T)) 

  I have two thoughts about how I should go about this
  1) write a new smoothing function (like ns or bs) that creates the
appropriate basis (which I have no idea how to do so any pointers would be
helpful) or
  2) muck about with the data a little by putting the last six months worth
of data on the front of the original series and first six months of data at
the end or it and do the modelling based on this doubled series. This would
mean mucking around with the variances to get the right test statistics at
the end.

  The first idea seems elegant but time consuming and the latter very
inelegant, mucky but useful as a hack.

  Does anyone have some other ideas or solutions? Or come across some
software that implements periodic smooths with gams in Splus?

  Any help would be muchly appreciated,
  Megan 

----

Biostatistician,                      http://www.ctru.auckland.ac.nz

Auckland, New Zealand.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Periodic Splines and Gams
messages.body_plain:
Consider that you may want to do something else. For some
diseases, the seasonality of incidence varies from year to year. For
example, there tends to be a two year cycle of influenza epidemics,
because if many people are infected in year 1, more partial immunity
exists in year 2. Also, the virulence of the virus varies from year to
year, and because of these two factors, the size of the winter peak varies
substantially. I do not know if this applies to your data. If so, you
might want to create a month of study variable, and smooth against that,
so that the seasonal patterns can vary from year to year. You can keep
this from getting out of hand by limiting the number of degrees of freedom
per year to 3-4. This works pretty well for pneumonia hospital admissions,
for example. 
 
Joel Schwartz

messages.body_plain:
Eric Elguero wonders:

> 
> >Yesterday I posted a question about extracting non null elements from a list.
> 
> (...)
> >Bill Venables: for (i in length(ttt):1) ttt[[i]] <- ttt[[i]]  # Note that the
> >loop starts from the end.
> >
> 
> I cannot figure out the logic behind this, but I noticed that the order of
> the operations doesn't matter.
> for (i in sample(length(ttt))... does the same.
> 
> 
> e.e.

(any relation to e e cummings?)

I'm glad it tweaked someone's curiosity.

The explanation comes from the fact that you can remove
components from a list by assign NULL to that position:

> m <- as.list(letters[1:3])
> m
[[1]]:
[1] "a"

[[2]]:
[1] "b"

[[3]]:
[1] "c"

> m[[1]] <- NULL
> m
[[1]]:
[1] "b"

[[2]]:
[1] "c"

My warning to work from the end back was unnecessary (as I should
have realised had I re-read my own homily on backout and all
that...) but harmless.

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Periodic Splines and Gams
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'd like to thanks heaps to all the people below who responded to my request -
Joel Schwartz, Richard Raubertas, Matthias Richard, Hong Ooi, Henrik
Aalborg Nielsen and Sama LowChoy

It was excellent posting on Friday night and then coming back the next
morning to  find so many people having taken the trouble to reply and
with some _great_ pointers as well.  :-> 

Most of these responses came through on the mail list so I'll only
mention the posts of Hong Ooi and Henrik Aalborg Nielsen which came to
me personally. Both mention locfit and Henrik Aalborg Nielsen (and
Richard Raubertas) pointed to an archieved posting that had previously
answered one of my questions (thanks to Douglas Bates/Henrik Aalborg 
Nielsen for that answer). 

==================================================================
Hong Ooi wrote:
The locfit package by Clive Loader has a facility for periodic smooths;
however the documentation is a bit sparse. You can download the code
from his web page, http://cm.bell-labs.com/stat/project/locfit. There
are versions for SPlus (3.x, 4.x/2000 and 5.x), R, and a standalone C
program.

There should also be a short introductory paper there on how to use the
package. If you're going to use locfit, though, you're probably best off
getting the Springer text as well: Loader, C (1999), _Local Regression
and Likelihood_, NY: Springer.

===================================================================
Henrik Aalborg Nielsen wrote:
LOCFIT once allowed the argument kt="ang" for smoothing measurements on
the unit circle.  I don't know if this works anymore - you might want to
look it up in Loaders book (see the LOCFIT homepage).  Anyway, this will
only handle the non-parametric part of the model and you will have to
program a loop doing backfitting and local scoring.  

LOCFIT can be found at:
http://cm.bell-labs.com/cm/ms/departments/sia/project/locfit/index.html

If you can accept that using a splines basis may move the hills and
valleys (Hastie & Tibshirani (1990), "Generalized Additive Models",
Section 9.3.5) you can use a periodic B-spline basis together with
glm().

In June last year Douglas Bates <bates at stat.wisc.edu> showed me how to
to make a periodic spline basis.  There is a summary at:

http://www.biostat.wustl.edu/s-news/s-news-archive/199906/msg00241.html

====================================================================

I have played a tiny bit with LOCFIT so far. The only thing worth
mentioning is that instead of typing kt="ang" as an argument in the
function call, the current notation should be y~ang(x) (with y being the
response and x the explanatory variable) i.e. it's now part of the formula.

Thanks all,
Megan

Hi all,
        I have a series data set that is corrupted, in a sense.  As an
example, the original data file may look like:

class   time
A        2
B        8
B        4
C        5
A        3
A        6

where time is in seconds and class is the characteristic in which I am
interested.  I would simply like to compute the number of times that each
class appears and the various durations associated with each
appearance.  The complication is in correcting the file to illustrate the 
true series:

class   time
A        2
B        12
C        5
A        9

Currently I loop over each row and compare the current class to the class
in the next row, if they are identical I sum the durations and represent
the sum with a single class designation in a new dataframe.  As you can
imagine for my set of 2000-4000 rows this takes some time.  
Are there any ideas to make the correction more efficient?

I am using S-PLUS 4.5 for the PC.

RC

messages.subject: [S] Re: using C with S-PLUS for Windows
messages.subject_clean: [S] Re: using C with S-PLUS for Windows
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 10 Apr 2000, Abhyuday Mandal wrote:

> we use SPlus4.5 (windows).
> I tried to call a c-function from splus. online help tells us to
> give the commands 
> 
> > dos("COMPILE myfun.c",out=F)        # C compiler produces myfun.obj
> > dyn.load("myfun.obj")       # dynamically load myfun.obj
> > .C("myfun",args)    # invoke the function>
> 
> to compile the function, we need to give "COMPILE ...", but for that it
> seems we need WATCOM which we do not have.  Nevertheless, we can get the
> object file by compiling externally, can't we ? but then the dyn.load
> command is not working.

You can compile externally, but you do need to use the COMPILE script (or
the flags it contains).

> do i absolutely need the watcom compiler and can i use turbo c / unix
> based compiler/gnu compiler, which i have, for this purpose. 

You EITHER absolutely need Watcom to use dyn.load (and Watcom has withdrawn
the compiler) OR you can use dll.load and make a DLL with almost any
Windows compiler.  See the S-PLUS Programmer's Guide!

Now, Turbo C is not AFAIK a Windows compiler that can build 32-bit Windows
DLLs (Borland C++ is), and you can't compile on Unix.  You can use the
mingw32 port of gcc: see the on-line V&R complements
(http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/MASS2/VR2sp4.pdf) or our new book
`S Programming' (to be published next week) for how to use this.

messages.subject: Re: [S] function's problems
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 10 Apr 2000, Siana Halim wrote:

> 
> Dear Users,
> 
> (1)   We got a problem to run functions saved in text (*.txt) files, 
> since we have a lot of functions that already saved in that format, and 
> we do not like to copy paste every function into fix() format.

Use source() to load them.

> (2)   How to access a function which is already in main function for 
> example :
>       function(m,n){
>        a <- function(n) {
>               a <- n^2
>          }
> 
>        cat(a(n))   # is not a problem but
>       
>        b <- function(m) {
>               b <- a(n) * 5  # the result is error "a is not recognized"
>          }
>         
>        }       

You need to read the S scope rules. Suppose the outer function is called
my. Then

my(2,3)

establishes frame 1, then frame 2 for my and frame 3 if my actually calls
b.  So a(n) is called in frame 3, and both a and n are defined in frame 2.

The scope rules are that evaluation in frame N looks in frame N then 1 then
0 then the search path. It does not look in N-1 down to 2.

I am not sure what you are trying to achieve by this, but for advanced S
programming like this you really need to understand the rules.

--

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Remote editing of graphics in Powerpoint
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Remote editing of graphics in Powerpoint
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all who responded.  In summary, editing
graphs in Powerpoint works reasonably well.
I have indicated some of my own comments in brackets [].

Michael Conklin   <mconklin at customresearch.com>

We send them to WMF files and import them to PowerPoint
to edit them there. Some of our clients have found that
using the PowerPoint presentation wizard in SPlus does
an even better job.  The big problem is distortion and
the tendancy of some Microsoft tools to reorient the
labels in the graphs.  [This problem is shared by
Metafile Companion - www.companionsoftware.com - which
is otherwise the easiest to use graphics editor I've
seen.]

Gina Lockwood <gina.lockwood at uhn.on.ca>

I have had great success with saving the S-Plus graph
as a windows metafile and editing it in PowerPoint. You
insert the graph as a picture; double click on the
graph and answer yes to the question about converting
to a Microsoft Office file. Then by clicking and
selecting various items you can change titles, fonts,
colours, and (God forbid) even the actual lines or bars
or data points. In some ways it allows the client too
much power.

Joseph C. Davis <jdavis at pdf.com>

I do this almost every day :-( Usually, it is easiest
to create teh basic graph in Splus, import into PPT and
then use the edit tools there. If you want to edit
things like the legends, etc, then there is only one
thing that I know of. If you double-click on a WMF
picture, it will ask you if you want to conver to some
sort of picture format. Say yes, and it converts to a
bunch of unit pieces which you can then edit. Painful,
but it works.

Brendan Wilson <wilsonb at netidea.com>

I occasionally copy and paste individual graphs
directly into Powerpoint. I resize the object and
choose its location, select the object, right click and
select the ungroup option. This allows me to edit each
"sub-object" from the original graph without S-plus
running. However, there are alignment problems with
some of the smaller objects like tick marks that I
haven't resolved adequately yet, and the resolution of
the underlying "snap to grid" location function in
Powerpoint is frustratingly coarse. Maybe you can
improve on this method.

James G. Herndon <jim at rmy.emory.edu>

If you use "Edit/Copy Graph sheet Page" in Splus 2000
for PC and then "Edit/Paste Special/Picture(Enhanced
Metafile)" in Powerpoint 2000, then the picture can be
edited in Powerpoint independently of Splus.

David Southerland <souther at knology.net>

    I've had marginal-to-adequate success in just
saving the graph as a .WMF file that I then insert into
a Microsoft Word document where I edit it.  When it
finally looks like I want then (after saving it first,
naturally) I copy it to the clipboard and then paste it
into Powerpoint.  I often have to change the
orientation of the y-axis and move the legend items a
bit, but it seems to work well enough that I haven't
tried using other programs (- well, other than just
reploting it in S-plus and then inserting the .WMF file
directly into PowerPoint).   I've been using Word 97
and Splus 2000.

    For simple graphs, I've often just exported the
reduced data in nice columns as a tab-delimited ASCII
file and let others just import the ASCII file into
Microsoft Excel (or whatever they like) where they can
use the plot wizard and do with it as they wish.  [The
main problem I've had with this approach is that we
plot a lot of step-function survival curves, and other
systems do not support step functions directly.]

    I seem to recall some people who would save the
plot as a Postscript file and then edit it in a
Postscript viewer, but I don't think that Joe Blow user
would find that palatable.  [I think this is probably
the most reliable approach when the object is to get a
nice printed document; it's just that you can't view
the postscript on the screen in Word, and I suspect
that Powerpoint won't like postscript files.  It may be
worth investigating postscript to wmf conversion.  You
can convert postscript to Adobe Illustrator using
Ghostscript and edit this using Mayura Draw
(www.mayura.com), then export to wmf.]

messages.subject: Re: [S] Downhill Simplex method for S-PLUS
messages.body_plain:
At 4/7/00 at 11:27 AM, Longhow Lam wrote:

> For those who are interested, you can now download an S-PLUS routine
> that minimizes an S-PLUS function using the downhill simplex method.
>
> The S-PLUS routine calls a C dll which does all the compuations. This
> dll is based on C code from Numerical Recipes.  [...]

Having used similar code in Fortran for over 10 years, perhaps I can add a 
mild warning, not about any particular code, but about the method 
itself.  Although it is remarkable for not blowing up on some extremely 
ugly (non-differentiable) objective functions, the downhill simplex 
(Nelder-Mead) method tends to stop at local minima.  This fact and the 
general outline of how to get around it (by restarting the algorithm) are 
given, though not prominently, in Numerical Recipes (the Fortran version, 
and probably also the C).

It would be easy to obtain plausible but incorrect results by ignoring this 
characteristic of the method.

I haven't examined the code generously provided by Longhow Lam, but if it 
doesn't take measures to ensure that its solution can not be bettered by 
repeated tries in the same neighborhood, such measures should be taken by 
the user.  There is no reason why such restarts should be considered part 
of the simplex implementation itself, but they should definitely be part of 
the surrounding user code.  (At least one implementation of the 
Nelder-Mead  fits a quadratic surface at the stopping point as such a 
measure, but last time I looked, this was not part of the Numerical Recipes 
code.  It might not be a good approach in all cases, e.g., if the objective 
function is not differentiable.)

--
Michael Prager, Ph.D.                <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>
NOAA Beaufort Laboratory
Beaufort, North Carolina  28516

messages.body_plain:
The dll that I provided does not do a restart. It starts from a starting
simplex and loops until it converges. You have to do a restart
"manually".

Not only does the Simplex method tends to stop at a local minimum it
just stops at a local minimum. And there is no way you can be sure that
it is global, other than restarting with different starting points.
Another good reason to restart (at the point where the method claimed it
has found a minimum) is that the convergence criteria might be fooled by
a single anomalous step that, for some reason or another, failed to get
anywhere.

Cheers,
Longhow

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Column names as arguments
messages.body_plain:
I thank all who replied.  E-mail exchanges with Peter Perkins, Bert Gunter, 
and Doug Bates were particularly helpful.

To repeat the original query briefly:

> Part of a function definition (line numbers added only here) is--

>

> 1 "get.bwplot" <- function(in.var)

> 2    {

> 3    # Make the actual plot:

> 4    Fred <- bwplot(cv.err  ~ in.var | alpha * m, data=all.e)

> 5    }

>

> When called with

>

>     get.bwplot(e.msy)

>

> (where e.msy is a column of data.frame all.e)

>

> this fails with an error like "Object in.var not found."  However, if

> "in.var" on line 4 is replaced with (not in quotes) "e.msy", the call 
succeeds.

This was identified by some as a scoping problem, and indeed the S-Plus 
scoping rules seem to be a source of many errors, by me and others.  In 
this case, however, the problem was something else: my failure to clearly 
differentiate between the name of an object and the object itself.

The first one to suggest a clear and workable solution was Peter Perkins, 
who pointed out that an S-Plus formula can be built up as a character 
string and then designated a formula with formula(), as in

        get.bwplot" <- function(in.var)
        var.name <- deparse(substitute(in.var)) ## Convert to character string
        my.form <- as.formula(paste("cv.err ~", var.name, "| alpha * m"))

and then used in something like

	bwplot(my.form, data=all.e)

That did the trick nicely.

--
Michael Prager, Ph.D.                <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>
NOAA Beaufort Laboratory
Beaufort, North Carolina  28516

messages.subject: [S] Summary: function's problems
messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot for Prof. Brian Riply and Dr. Heisterkamp for the reply.

here is the summary of their answer.. 

siana
------------

On Mon, 10 Apr 2000, Prof Brian D Ripley wrote:

> On Mon, 10 Apr 2000, Siana Halim wrote:
> 
> > 
> > Dear Users,
> > 
> > (1) We got a problem to run functions saved in text (*.txt) files, 
> > since we have a lot of functions that already saved in that format, and 
> > we do not like to copy paste every function into fix() format.
> 
> Use source() to load them.
> 
> > (2) How to access a function which is already in main function for 
> > example :
> >     function(m,n){
> >      a <- function(n) {
> >             a <- n^2
> >          }
> > 
> >      cat(a(n))   # is not a problem but
> >     
> >      b <- function(m) {
> >             b <- a(n) * 5  # the result is error "a is not recognized"
> >          }
> >         
> >        }     
> 
> You need to read the S scope rules. Suppose the outer function is called
> my. Then
> 
> my(2,3)
> 
> establishes frame 1, then frame 2 for my and frame 3 if my actually calls
> b.  So a(n) is called in frame 3, and both a and n are defined in frame 2.
> 
> The scope rules are that evaluation in frame N looks in frame N then 1 then
> 0 then the search path. It does not look in N-1 down to 2.
> 
> I am not sure what you are trying to achieve by this, but for advanced S
> programming like this you really need to understand the rules.
> 
> -- 
> Brian D. Ripley,                  ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk
> Professor of Applied Statistics,  http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~ripley/
> University of Oxford,             Tel:  +44 1865 272861 (self)
> 1 South Parks Road,                     +44 1865 272860 (secr)
> Oxford OX1 3TG, UK                Fax:  +44 1865 272595
> 
> 
------------------------------
just put on each line with the function definition with a text editor

myname<-function(.........

then use in s-plus :
source("file name of the text file")

note:
 you could have prevented this situation by using dump()!     

Dr.S.H Heisterkamp

Hi folks,

Although a longtime Stata user, I am new to s-plus. I am the using s-plus
2000 for Windows.  I would like to make better use of the interface.

Selection of variables for a dialog boxes.
  
dialog boxes in the stats section are too small to effectively select
variables, especially when the dataset contains hundreds of variables. 
I've learned that I can use the object explorer instead.  Even this can be
cumbersome when one has to scroll hundreds of variables.  It is a there a
trick in s-plus for restricting the number of variables available for
analysis?  For example, say one wanted to analyze 10 of 200 variables
during a session:

only these few variables?  I've tried this, but when I try to keep only of
the variables of interest by deleting the shortcuts to the other
variables, s-plus deletes them both from the new page or folder and from
the original.  I've also tried copying of the database itself.  The
problem with this if it is that if one updates one copy, one has to
remember to update the other.

2.      Is there an s-plus command which performs this 'filtering' on
variable names?

3.      How can one construct a data frame containing only these
variables? (the disadvantage here is having too many structures containing
the same data).

Thanks for your help.

messages.body_plain:
Peter Ellis writes:

> 
> I'm interested in the answer to the second part of Vito's question.  I'm sure
> I've read that the following two calls are meant to be equivalent (where y is
> the vector of number of successes from the vector n of group sizes):
> 
> glm(y~x,family=binomial,weights=n)
> glm(cbind(y,n-y)~x,family=binomial)
> 
> but only the second version gives what I consider the correct residual 
> deviance,
> etc, even when (sorry I don't have the example on my box here) with other data
> sets I don't get the warning messages Vito did on the first call and in fact 
> get
> _coefficient estimates_ which are close to those from the second call.
> 

There are two issues here.

1. the formula in the first style of call should be  

        y/n ~ x 

rather than y ~ x.  That is, in this style of call the response
is a proportion (or binary) rather than a frequency.

2. there has been, since the first release of the software around
10 years ago, a bug in the fitting program in that if you fit the
model in the first form it seems to start from the wrong starting
point.  You can see this be setting a trace.  Here is an example:

> kalythos
  Age  N Blind 
1  20 50     6
2  35 50    17
3  45 50    26
4  55 50    37
5  70 50    44
> fm <- glm(Blind/N ~ Age, binomial, kalythos, weights=N, trace=T)
GLM    linear loop 1: deviance = 3.266 
GLM    linear loop 2: deviance = 0.3549 
GLM    linear loop 3: deviance = 0.3171 
GLM    linear loop 4: deviance = 0.3171 
> gm <- glm(cbind(Blind, N-Blind) ~ Age, binomial, kalythos, trace=T)
GLM    linear loop 1: deviance = 0.3181 
GLM    linear loop 2: deviance = 0.3171 
GLM    linear loop 3: deviance = 0.3171 

Notice how they both end up with the same deviance, but the first
fit takes four steps rather than three and the first step is far
from a good starting point and the second is still relatively 
poor.

It mostly does not matter, since the algorthym seems to be robust
enough to recover from a dramatically bad starting point but
conceivably it could matter in some circumstances.  For safety's
sake I would suggest always using the second form.

[Maybe if enough people send a note to bugs at statsci.com they
might eventually sort it out.  There is no reason why the two
should behave any differently at all.]

Bill Venables.
--

On Tue, 11 Apr 2000, Peter Ellis wrote:

> sets I don't get the warning messages Vito did on the first call and in fact

> _coefficient estimates_ which are close to those from the second call.
> 
> Grateful any comments.  

(a) They are meant to fit the same model *if* y is the proportion in the
first case and the count in the second. So one should get

> glm(y/n~x,family=binomial,weights=n)                                  
Call:
glm(formula = y/n ~ x, family = binomial, weights = n)

Coefficients:
 (Intercept)          x 
    1.321256 -0.8896124

Degrees of Freedom: 3 Total; 1 Residual
Residual Deviance: 0.05325231 
> glm(cbind(y,n-y)~x,family=binomial)
Call:
glm(formula = cbind(y, n - y) ~ x, family = binomial)

Coefficients:
 (Intercept)          x 
    1.321256 -0.8896124

Degrees of Freedom: 3 Total; 1 Residual
Residual Deviance: 0.05325231 

(b) They use different starting values. The code is

> binomial()$initialize
expression({
        if(is.matrix(y)) {
                if(dim(y)[2] > 2)
                        stop("only binomial response matrices (2 columns)")
                n <- drop(y %*% c(1, 1))
                y <- y[, 1]
        }
        else {
                if(is.category(y))
                        y <- y != levels(y)[1]
                else y <- as.vector(y)
                n <- rep(1, length(y))
        }
        w <- w * n
        n[n == 0] <- 1
        y <- y/n
        mu <- y + (0.5 - y)/n
}
)

In the first case n=1 and the start (mu) is at 0.5. In the second n=50 and
the start is at 0.2 0.4 0.6.

The fix is to replace

        else {
                if(is.category(y))
                        y <- y != levels(y)[1]
                else y <- as.vector(y)
                n <- rep(1, length(y))

by something like

        else {
                if(is.category(y)) {
                        y <- y != levels(y)[1]
                        n <- rep(1, length(y))
                } else {
                        y <- as.vector(y)
                        n <- rep(w, len=length(y))
                }

>    (Intercept)         x1
> x1 -0.9995754
> x2 -0.9989584   0.9992285
> Warning messages:
>   linear convergence not obtained in  10  iterations. in: glm.fitter(x = X,
> y = Y, w = w, start = start, offset = offset, family =   ...
> >
> 
> Of course the ML estimate don't exist (am I right?) and so the results are 
> wrong, 

Let me say again: ML estimate of what? There is an MLE of the fitted
values, and glm finds it (to machine tolerance). Try

> fitted(glm(y/n~x,family=binomial,weights=n))
   1   2            3 
 0.8 0.6 1.363478e-05

What do you think is wrong in the results?

> but conditional exact inference is avaible (p-value an CI). Is 
> possible to get a bootstrap estimate too? I'm not absolutely expert in 
> resample problems, so probably it's a silly question.

Try setting contrasts to see this more clearly:

options(contrasts=c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))
xx <- factor(3:1, levels=3:1)
glm(y/n~xx,family=binomial,weights=n)

Coefficients:
 (Intercept)        xx2       xx1 
    1.386294 -0.9808293 -12.58917

Degrees of Freedom: 3 Total; 0 Residual
Residual Deviance: 0.001363487 

and the last coefficient should be -Inf in the MLE.

> summary(.Last.value)

Coefficients:
                  Value Std. Error    t value 
(Intercept)   1.3862944  0.3535534  3.9210326
        xx2  -0.9808293  0.4564355 -2.1488892
        xx1 -12.5891676 23.2326690 -0.5418735

Now, what do you want to do inference on?  Anything you do here on all but
xx1 will be fine with glm. I don't think bootstrap sampling of the MLE is
going to be of any help, as the bootstrap distribution will always select
failures at level x=1 (that's all you have observed) and the MLE for xx1
will still be -Inf.

In this example what you really have is 50 failures in one group of
a binomial.  So the problem is given  X ~ bin(50, p), observe X=0,
do inference on p.  The glm answer is silly, as the local linear
approximation breaks down.  You can do exact inference, though, as you say.

--

filenames<- c(paste("d:\\ana\\", 9505:9509, ".dbf", sep=""))

messages.body_plain:
I am dealing with a some piecewise quadratic functions of the form:

function( x, mu, lamda, sigma.rho, cost, y) {
# x, mu and cost are vectors of length N
# sigma.rho is a symetric positive semi-definite
# matrix of dimension N

retval <- sum( x * mu) + lamda * as.double( t(x) %*% sigma.rho %*% x) + sum( 
cost * abs(x-y))

return (retval)
}

Possible constraints on x are, sum(x) <= a, max(abs(x)) <= b, or maybe sum( 
x^2)<=c

I will need to solve for the minimum, any where from a few hundred times to a 
few thousand times.

I could use the mls function, but it is a bit clunky to implement domain 
constraints, and check for convergance. Does anybody have any suggestions?

Thanks in Advance,

Clark Sims

messages.body_plain:
Dear S-users,

I couldn't figure out an answer to a question and so decide to ask
for help. I have a data set in event history format like this:

                   y    x1    x2    x3
obs1(year1964)     0    22    40    9
obs1(year1965)     0    24    41    8
obs1(year1966)     1    20    35    11
...
obs1(year1994)     1    17    40    8
obs2(year1964)
obs2(year1965)
obs2(year1966)
...

around 500 obervations, each with 31 years data

y tells essentially when an event happens (so it happened in 1966 for
obs1). I just want to fit a parametric model (with a Weibull baseline, for
example). I could use survreg, but so I have to change the data structure
into Surv(time, cens). I could do so with quite some effort, but then how
could I take into account of the fact that x's change over time? Actually
am I on the wrong track to try parametric models with changing causal
variables?

Your help is much appreciated. Thanks.

Sincerely,

Man-shan Kwok
Princeton University

messages.subject: [S] Terry Therneau Survival Course - Offered by MathSoft
messages.subject_clean: [S] Terry Therneau Survival Course - Offered by MathSoft
messages.body_plain:
Modeling Survival Data: Extending the Cox Model
presented by:  Terry Therneau, Ph.D.
Chicago, IL
May 22-23, 2000

MathSoft is offering the course Modeling Survival Data: Extending the Cox
Model, a two day training course presented by Terry Therneau, Ph.D., in
Chicago, IL  -  May 22-23, 2000.

Due to the short notice of this course, we are offering a one-time
discounted rate of:

Cost     $795    Commercial/Government/Academic

Registration/Questions:
Phone:  Cathie Lynch at 800-569-0123 x246
Email: clynch at splus.mathsoft.com
Web:  http://www.splus.mathsoft.com/splus/train/2000schedule.htm

Course Description:
During the last 2-3 years the survival analysis software available in
several of the standard statistical packages has experienced a major
increment in functionality, and is no longer limited to the triad
of Kaplan-Meier curves, logrank tests, and simple Cox models. Many
of these new techniques can be formulated as extensions or
enhancements to the standard Cox regression programs such as phreg (SAS).

The theory behind many of these methods is closely related to the theory
of counting processes, as set forth in the books by Fleming and Harrington
and Andersen et al., giving them a solid mathematical underpinning.
Although they are of significant practical worth, many of the
techniques are little utilized, however, because of the perception
that specialized programming or software is required. The exposition
will focus on three aspects: heuristic explanations of the methods,
actual data examples that utilize each of them, and the SAS and/or
S-Plus code to implement the examples.

Mathematical detail is supplied only when necessary.

Objectives:

Topics will include:
The counting process form of a Cox model, and its use for:
        left truncation
            disjoint intervals of risk
            time dependent strata
            multiple time scales
Expected survival curves
The use of residuals for:
        estimation of functional form
            assessment of proportional hazards via time-dependent
coefficients
            assessment of leverage
Robust variance estimation
Case-cohort designs
The analysis of multiple events/subject

Audience:

The examples are drawn from medical research in cancer and transplantation,
using both clinical
trials and natural history studies. Attendees should have a basic
familiarity with survival analysis
techniques. Familiarity with either SAS or S-PLUS will be useful.

Outline:

1. Preliminaries Notation and conventions to be used Five minute
introductions to S-Plus and SAS
(enough to read the overheads) Definition of the Cox model Simple Cox
models; the coxph()function
stratification variables log likelihood, score, and Wald tests handling of
ties infinite coefficients Sample size

2. The counting process form of a Cox model Mathematics History Particular
examples Time dependent
covariates Discontinuous intervals of risk Multiple time scales Time
dependent strata Implementation
in SAS and S Examples Stanford heart transplant Parkinson's disease Mortgage
terminations Cystic fibrosis

3. Residuals for Cox models

        Notation Martingale and deviance residuals Score residuals
        Schoenfeld residuals General residuals. What can we test in a Cox model?

4. Estimation of functional form Simple martingale residuals Using a null
model Using a fitted model
        Deficiencies Extensions

        Improved martingale residuals Relationship to Poisson regression
Regression splines and
          smoothing splines
        Examples Primary biliary cirrhosis Veterans Administration data
        Time dependent covariates

5. Time dependent coefficient models As a test for proportional hazards
Estimation using scaled Schoenfeld
residuals Plots Choice of time scale, relationship to other tests Examples
Simulation Veterans Administration
data

6. Leverage and robust variance Leverage Jackknife Approximate jackknife
methods Example: PBC data
Robust variance estimation jackknife grouped jackknife relationship to
sandwich estimates and other methods

7. Multiple and correlated events Methods - Time to first event - Special
time-dependent covariates - Random
effects models - Marginal models

        Motivation for the marginal model
            Simple examples: Doubled data Delayed second event
            Model choices Ordered events vs unordered events Time scales
Strata
        Time-dependent covariates Counting process form
        Models Andersen-Gill Marginal Conditional
            Particular cases - Different types of event: PBC UDCA study -
Multiple occurrence:
        rhDNase study Gamma interferon Bladder cancer study - Paired events:
Diabetic retinopathy
            study Survival and progression in colon cancer
            Complex examples Homeless and shelter Multiple states in
Inflamatory Bowel Disease

8. Random effects or "frailty" models Relationship to penalized models
Gamma random effects Gaussian random effects Degrees of freedom Examples
Rats Colon cancer Gamma interferon study Center-specific treatment
effects Hospital profiling

9. Expected survival Predicted survival from a Cox model Fixed covariates
Time-dependent covariates Population rate tables Individual expected
survival vs cohort survival Three estimates of cohort survival
Ederer or exact method Hakulinen estimate Conditional method The survexp
function Using expected survival in person-years models

10. Weighted sampling Survey designs Binder's variance estimate
Case-cohort designs motivation relationship to survey sampling variants
computation of estimate and variances
        Nested case-control

11. Accelerated failure time models Definition Fitting Residuals Advantages
and disadvantages with respect to a Cox model Examples Environment and
genetic factors in the risk of breast cancer
Effect of rheumatoid arthritis on cardiac disease

12. Summary

messages.subject: [S] problems using time series object "its"
messages.body_plain:
I've just started using "its" objects, but am finding several problems
using them:

(1) ts.plot() does not print dates on the horiz axis in a useful way (e.g.,
when plotting a timeseries object with consecutive days, all I get printed
is the year, which is the same for every day & is not useful)(2) apply()
produces superfluous warning messages when apply a function to the columns
of an its object

Here's a brief example that illustrates both these problems:

x <- structure(.Data = c(0, 0, 1, 3, 1, 7, 6, 4, 7, 2, 0, 0, 8, 4, 2, 2,
11, 0, 4, 0, 0, 0, 3, 5, 5,
        2, 7, 8, 2, 0), .Dim = c(10, 3), .Dimnames = list(c("08/01/1999",
"08/02/1999", 
        "08/03/1999", "08/04/1999", "08/05/1999", "08/06/1999", "08/07/1999",
"08/08/1999", 
        "08/09/1999", "08/10/1999"), c("3700000552", "3700030366", 
"3700030373")),
tspar = 
        structure(.Data = c(14457, 14458, 14459, 14460, 14461, 14462, 14463,
14464, 14465, 
        14466), format = "m/d/year", origin = structure(.Data = c(1, 1, 1960),
.Names = c(
        "month", "day", "year")), class = c("dates", "times")), class = "its")

# prints only the year as labels on the x axis
ts.plot(x)

# [.its gives warnings as it extracts each column
xmax <- apply(x, 2, max)

I have fixed both of these problems by modifying ts.plot() and [.its(), but
I was wondering if there was a better way.

I'm using Splus Professional Rev 2 (5 Nov 99) under WindowsNT.

-- Tony Plate

-----------------------
Tony.Plate at biosgroup.com

messages.body_plain:
I don't know your data, but I can tell you something about selecting df in 
each smoothed variable by means of AIC, i.e. by using step.gam.

Sometime the AIC select too many df and so the almost the all variability of 
the response variable is "captured" by the smoothed terms.

You can see this by increasing or decreasing df in smoothing term: the t 
value for the other explanotary variables should decrease or increase: this 
is the problem when you use smoothing terms.

You can try BIC instead, just modify step.gam() or if you know whether exist 
an alternative function in s-plus.

I think this is the problem, but is there any further comment about this 
topic?
