messages.subject: [S] Answers to lme replicates questions
messages.body_plain:
I am very grateful to Jose’ Pinheiro for his 
helpful remarks regarding my lme questions. His 
answers are below followed by my original 
question:

Dear Ronald,

I am not sure I understood your description of 
the data structure
properly: my understanding is that you want to 
add an extra level of
nesting to the data and that there will be 
several observations made
at the "sub-side" level. If that's the case, 
your specification of the
the groupedData object is correct, that is, you 
should specify the
three levels of nesting in the display formula, 
        
pixel ~ day | dog / side / sub-side

> Question 1: what would be the plot statement?

For multilevel data as you described, there 
isn't a single meaningful
way to plot the data. You can look at the data 
at several levels (for
example, a curve for each dog, with the pixel 
intensity measurements
averaged over side and sub-side. Or you could 
preserve the dog and
side levels and look at different curves for 
each sub-side.). You can
use the arguments displayLevel and collapseLevel 
to specify different
plots. The default plot, obtained with 

 plot(pixel)

will display a different curve for each 
combination of
dog/side/sib-side. 

> Question 2: how do I arrange my data?

In the way you described. The different grouping 
variables must be
given as different columns in the data. 

> Question 3: do I need to include "sub-side" in 
> the fit model, or is that automatically done?

If you want random effects at the sub-side 
level, you will need to
declare it in the model, unless you want the 
same random effects to be
used at all levels of nesting (the default is to 
get the grouping
structure from the groupedData object, when none 
is specified. If no
random effects are specified, all fixed effects 
are assumed to have
random components - which will be repeated for 
all levels of nesting.)
Since this may result in too many random effects 
being used in the
model, it's probably a good idea to specify a 
more parsimonious
random effects model. 

> Suppose that the right side got a treatment 
and 
> the left side served as control, would the 
> following model be legitimate?
> 
> pixel.fit <- lme (fixed = pixel ~ day * side, 
> data = Pixel, random = dog ~ day)

The fixed-effects model is probably what you 
want, but the random
effects model is not. You don't specify the 
grouping variable on the
left hand side of the formula. You should use 
the | operator for that,
like in 
        
random = ~ day | dog

This statement will result in only two random 
effects (the intercept
and the day slope) at the dog level. If you want 
to have random
intercepts at the side and sub-side levels, for 
example, you should
use 
        
random = list(dog = ~dog, side = ~1, sub-side = 
~1)

Hope this helps,

--Jose'

messages.subject: [S] Passing NULLs to .C
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm writing a function in Splus which calls some C code. Some of the
arguments to the S function are optional, and I thought it would be
convenient just to assign them NULLs when they're not specified. The
code looks something like this:

[in S]

myfunc <- function(x, y, z = NULL) # x, y, z can be vectors
{
  ...
  ...
  .C("my_routine", x, y, z, as.integer(length(x)))
}

[in C]

void my_routine(double *x, double *y, double *z, long *n)
{
  ...
  ...
  if (/* a NULL was passed in z */) /* how to do this test? */
    do_something();
  else
    do_something_else();
  ...
} 

My question is, how are NULL values treated by .C() and/or .Fortran()?
At first I thought a NULL in S would correspond to a null pointer in C,
but some testing quickly disabused me of that notion. I can't seem to
find any docs on this either.

(I'm using Splus 2000 on Win98, and the C code is in a DLL compiled in
MS VC++ 6.)

Thanks,
Hong

--

Stop right there!  You need to ensure that x, y, z are doubles when
you pass them through .C, so you need as.double(x) etc.  Now NULL
is of mode NULL and as.double(NULL) is 0 on 3.4 and 5.1 at least.

> }

> find any docs on this either.
> 
> (I'm using Splus 2000 on Win98, and the C code is in a DLL compiled in
> MS VC++ 6.)

I would suggest passing missing values as NAs, but I am not sure that
compiler can cope properly with NaNs.  (Actually, I am sure it
can't but don't know whether this affects you.)   You need to use
S-PLUS macros to test for NA when you get to C: this is in the
Programmer's Guide.

#include <S.h>

   if(is_nan(x, DOUBLE))
      do_something();
   else
     do_something_else();

should do it for you.

Users of 5.1 can use .Call and pass NULLs.

 tr <- is.null(z)
 .C("my_routine", x, y, z, as.integer(length(x)), as.integer(tr))

void my_routine(double *x, double *y, double *z, long *n, long *tr)
 {

   ...

function estimation context) is well-known in the model selection
literature. You might want to look at a paper I wrote with Chih-Ling Tsai

Graphical Statistics, 8, 22-40 (1999). The paper gives a link to S-Plus
functions to use the method, which are available at my home page.

messages.subject_clean: [S] Question about GAM Model Selection using AIC
messages.body_plain:
If you are speaking about the smoothed terms, the answer is clear.
AIC might find that s(x,df=n) is significant as a predictor. However,
summary.glm displays a coefficient, standard error, and t statistic for
the linear part of the nonlinear fit. There is no reason that this should
be statistically significant just because the overall nonlinear fit is. 
        Would this be a good time to point out that statistical
significance is a poor reed for determining model fits. There is a good
history of simulations showing that stepwise regression to decide among
correlated covariates performs pretty poorly, and often chooses the
"wrong" variable. Also, variables may be insignificant because of lack of
power in the study, but still be predictors. If there is good
evidence  from past
studies to believe a variable is a predictor of your outcome, you should
probably include it in any case. 
Joel

messages.body_plain:
> Date: Wed, 12 Apr 2000 10:13:40 -0400 (EDT)
> From: Jeff Simonoff <jsimonof at stern.nyu.edu>

> This tendency for AIC to overfit (undersmooth in the nonparametric
> function estimation context) is well-known in the model selection
> literature. 

And earlier and in more detail in the time series literature in which it
arose.  It depends on the problem: AIC was designed to choose a model
with good prediction, and for AR(p) for example asymptotically
chooses a p at least as large as the true one (assumed to exist).
The TS people have lots of corrected versions.  For prediction
mild over-fitting is better than mild under-fitting, normally.

One problem with AIC is that it is derived assuming the models are all
true!  As a result, it is a biased estimate of the quantity it is 
trying to minimize for models smaller than the true model (if there
is a nested sequence and a true model).  Corrections such as NIC and 
p_eff reduce that effect.

--

messages.subject: [S] Regression tree significance tests?
messages.body_plain:
I've never used a regression tree before, but a quick look at the
description in Venables & Ripley suggests they might be useful for an
application I have.  In particular, suppose I have data with N cases,
each case having two explanatory variables, x1 and x2, and a response y.
I expect the relationships to be non-linear.

It appears easy enough with s-plus to fit a regression tree to these
data.  Would it then be possible to take a new data point (xn1, xn2, yn)
and to develop a significance test to ask whether that new point
belongs in a different population.  (I guess this "failure to belong"
may be too vague a concept.  I have to say that I generally don't like
significance tests at all, but this application falls in a context where
they are required by regulations.)  If anyone knows of such tests, I
would appreciation references to them.

Finally, to take this question a bit farther, if such tests do exist,
how might I determine their power?  Specifically, how might I estimate
the power for a case where xp1 and xp2 coincided with the x's from one
of the original cases, but yp deviated from the corresponding original y 
by some specified amount.

Please reply to me directly, and I'll summarize to the list.

Thanks for any help.

Dave Parkhurst

>        scales=list(y=list(las=0,at=c(2,14),labels=c(2,14))))
> 
> Here however las=0 does not work. Everything is back to the trellis
> default. What's going wrong ?

las does not work with axis when labels are specified: use srt-90 instead.
See help(axis) (but it is far from obvious as to why you need to
look at that).

messages.subject: [S] Memory problems, a soulution using Perl and S-PLUS
messages.subject_clean: [S] Memory problems, a soulution using Perl and S-PLUS
messages.body_plain:
Disclaimer:  I don't speak officially for MathSoft, this is a solution
that I found works, but is not the final word on the matter.  I hope this
helps some people, but it won't work for everybody (I can't even guarentee
that it will work for anybody).

Many people want to use S-PLUS to do simulations or iterative batch
runs that often consume large amounts of memory.  A couple of recent
posts on S-news have been on this topic.

This post is intended partly as a response to that post (one option)
as well as to give some general information.

The reason that S-PLUS sometimes has problems with some loops,
simulations, and long running batch processes is that is saves
information on how to back out of what has been done if there is a
problem.  This is a good thing for many cases, but can cause problems
with running a memory intensive function repetitively (because the
memory for allocated at each iteration is not reused in future
iterations).  This is not a problem when working interactively
executing one command at a time, because S-PLUS sees that the command
succeeded and that the undo information is no longer needed and that
the memory can be reused.

That means that if we can trick S-PLUS into thinking that commands are
being executed interactively, the memory will be reclaimed and the
simulations will run much longer and quicker without using up all
available memory.  Warning: while this is useful for some things, it
does circumvent useful features that were put there for a reason.

One approach is to use Perl to control a sub process of S-PLUS (I use
Perl because it is what I know, there are probably similar things
that can be done using Python, or C, or other languages).  For more
information of Perl, go to www.perl.com.  Perl is available for Unix
and Windows (I have used these methods on both).  The versions shown
below are for my Windows setup, just change the paths for your
Windows/Unix setup.

Perl's open command can be used to run a subprocess and pipe
information to it.  That is the method that will be described here.
Perl can also read information from a pipe or if special care is
taken, it can both write to and read from a subprocess.  For this
example we will limit ourselves to writing to the subprocess and
capturing the output into a file.

A simple Perl program that will take an S-PLUS batch file and run it
so that S-PLUS thinks that it is run interactively is:

-------------start script----------------------

#!/usr/local/bin -w
# the above line may need to be modified to match you settings if 
# running on Unix.

use strict;

open( SPLUS, '|"d:/Program Files/sp2000/cmd/sqpe" > output.txt' ) or 
      die "Could not open pipe: $!\n";
# this runs S-PLUS (actually sqpe a smaller text only version) and sets
# up the filehandle SPLUS so that anything that get printed to SPLUS 
# actually gets sent to the sqpe program as standard input.

print SPLUS <<EOS;
options(echo=T)
EOS
# put any initialization commands that you want above (before the EOS line)

while (<>){ # read a line from standard input (the batch function)
            # and put it into the special variable $_

  print SPLUS $_;
}

print SPLUS <<EO2;
q()
EO2
# put any clean-up above

close(SPLUS) or die "Problem closing pipe: $!\n";
# Test the close in case something went wrong before now.

------------ end script ---------------
  
It is that simple, just run it at the command line by typing:

perl batch.pl myjob.txt

where batch.pl is the above script and myjob.txt is your S-PLUS batch
file.

If you want to use for loops (even nested) then you can move these for
loops to the perl program.  Here is an example, where "myfunc" is a
simulation function that takes arguments beta, n, and sigma, simulates
some data analyses it, and returns a vector of length 6 as output.

--------start script------------
#!/usr/local/bin -w

use strict;

@beta_vals = (1,2,5,10,50,100);
@n_vals = (10,25,50,100,500);
@sigma_vals = (1,2,4,8);
# Set the parameters to simulate over

open( SPLUS, '|"d:/Program Files/sp2000/cmd/sqpe" > output.txt' ) or 
      die "Could not open pipe: $!\n";

print SPLUS <<EOS;
options(echo=T)
EOS

for my $beta ( @beta_vals ){
  for my $n ( @n_vals ){
    for my $sigma ( @sigma_vals ){

      $var_name = "sim.$beta.$n.$sigma";
      
      print SPLUS "$var_name <- matrix(NA, ncol=6, nrow=100)\n";
      # initialize matrix to end size

      for my $i (1..100){
        print SPLUS $var_name."[$i,] <- myfunc($beta,$n,$sigma)\n";
      }
    }
  }
}

print SPLUS "date()\nq()\n";

close(SPLUS) or die "Problem closing pipe: $!\n";

--------------end script--------------------

If myfunc uses a lot of memory and this were tried completely inside
S-PLUS, then all memory would soon be used up.  But running the above
command (perl batch2.pl) will not use much more memory than a single
run of myfunc.  The final results are stored in matrices who's name is
the 3 letters "sim" followed by the run conditions for that set of
runs.

One warning (discovered through experience), if a run of myfunc
results in an error, the seed will be reset so that the next run uses
the same random numbers and cause the error again and again until
S-PLUS stops from to many errors in a row.  You can generate a random
number before each run to generate a new seed, but this will make
tracking down the error much harder.

I hope that these 2 short scripts (and modifications of them) can help
people get around their memory problems with running simulations in
S-PLUS.

     (Greg)                  |   Love makes the trip worth taking.

messages.subject: RE: [S] Hilbert transform
messages.body_plain:
Alexander,

There is an fft function, so you can do the Hilbert transform by hand as
follows.

x<-seq(0,2*pi,len=129)[-129]
y<-cos(2*x)
n <- length(x)
hilb <- c(1,rep(-1i,n/2-1),1,rep(1i,n/2-1))
yhilb <- fft(hilb * fft(y,inverse=T)/length(y),inverse=T)
plot(x,y,type='l')
lines(x,Re(yhilb),col=2)

The help on fft doesn't give the format of the data after transformation, so
you have to figure it out by inspection. If x has length n then fft(x) is a
complex vector of length n (so there is two-fold redundancy), and

x[1] is the zero frequency component

if n is even
x[2] ... x[n/2] are the positive frequencies
x[n] ... x[n/2+2] are the negative frequencies and
x[n/2+1] is the Nyquist frequency

if n is odd
x[2] ... x[(n+1)/2] are the positive frequencies
x[n] ... x[(n+1)/2+1] are the negative frequencies and
there is no Nyquist frequency

See examples with pure cosine waves below to verify this.

Nick Ellis
CSIRO Marine Research   mailto:Nick.Ellis at marine.csiro.au
PO Box 120                      ph    +61 (07) 3826 7260
Cleveland QLD 4163      fax   +61 (07) 3826 7222
Australia                       http://www.marine.csiro.au

messages.subject: Re: [S] Passing NULLs to .C
messages.body_plain:
I'd like to say thanks to Prof Brian Ripley and Longhow Lam for their
replies to my query. Bill Dunlap also sent an informative reply, which
I'm forwarding to the list with his permission.

On Wed, 12 Apr 2000 13:22:31 -0700 (PDT), Bill Dunlap <bill at statsci.com>
wrote:

>On Wed, 12 Apr 2000, Prof Brian Ripley wrote:
>
>> > From: Hong Ooi <hong.ooi at wintermute.anu.edu.au>
>> > To: s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
>> > 
>> > I'm writing a function in Splus which calls some C code. Some of the
>> > arguments to the S function are optional, and I thought it would be
>> > convenient just to assign them NULLs when they're not specified. The
>> > code looks something like this:
>> > 
>> > 
>> > [in S]
>> > 
>> > myfunc <- function(x, y, z = NULL) # x, y, z can be vectors
>> > {
>> >   ...
>> >   ...
>> >   .C("my_routine", x, y, z, as.integer(length(x)))
>> 
>> Stop right there!  You need to ensure that x, y, z are doubles when
>> you pass them through .C, so you need as.double(x) etc.  Now NULL
>> is of mode NULL and as.double(NULL) is 0 on 3.4 and 5.1 at least.
>
>as.double(NULL) is numeric(0), a zero long vector of doubles.  If
>you pass that to C it will be passed as a double* but that pointer
>will not point to anything useful (it will not be a 0 pointer
>either).  Right now it will probably point to a zero, but that may
>change in the future.
>
>> I would suggest passing missing values as NAs, but I am not sure that
>> compiler can cope properly with NaNs.  (Actually, I am sure it
>> can't but don't know whether this affects you.)   You need to use
>> S-PLUS macros to test for NA when you get to C: this is in the
>> Programmer's Guide.
>> 
>> #include <S.h>
>> 
>>    if(is_nan(x, DOUBLE))
>>       do_something();
>>    else
>>      do_something_else();
>> 
>> should do it for you.
>
>Yes, you can use NA or some other special flag value to mean that
>the parameter's value is not meaningful (and thus use a default value
>or some other algorithm).  I would use is_na(x,DOUBLE) instead of
>is_nan(x,DOUBLE) as that will catch just the NA value and not any
>old NaN (the NaN's may arise for other reasons).
>
>----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>Bill Dunlap                                      22461 Mt Vernon-Big Lake Rd
>Data Analysis Products Div. of MathSoft, Inc.    Mount Vernon, WA 98274
>bill at statsci.com                                 360-428-8146
>

messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary+small follow-up: strange behaviour of dates
messages.body_plain:
Last Monday I asked the following question:

> Is there any logic behind the following behaviour?
> First create vector of dates
>  b<-dates(c("03/11/1990",NA,"09/29/1992"))
> 
> > min(b,dates("02/01/1988"))
> [1] 02/01/1988
> > min(c(b,dates("02/01/1988")))
> [1] 02/01/1988
> and also
> 
> > min(b,as.numeric(dates("02/01/1988")))
> [1] 02/01/1988
> > min(c(b,as.numeric(dates("02/01/1988"))))
> [1] 02/01/1988
> 
> Why are missings ignored in "min" if one of the objects is of class dates?

I received one answer, from Bill Dunlap, saying it is a bug in S-PLUS.
His answer is attached below.

Another unexpected thing (to me at least) happened with the following dates
manipulation:
> e<-ifelse(is.na(b),dates("02/01/1988"),b)
> e
[1] 11027 10258 11960
attr(, "format"):
[1] "m/d/year"
attr(, "origin"):
 month day year 
     1   1 1960
> class(e)
NULL

Of course, the dates class can easily be restored via dates(e), but it
woulde be nicer if it would not get lost in the ifelse construction.

Ronald Geskus

Municipal Health Service
  dept. VGZM
Nieuwe Achtergracht 100
1018 WT Amsterdam
Netherlands
tel. 31 20 555 5524
fax  31 20 555 5533
email: rgeskus at gggd.amsterdam.nl

Until June 30 at:
Service d'Epidémiologie - INSERM U292
Hôpital de Bicêtre
82 rue du Général Leclerc
94276 Le Kremlin-Bicêtre Cedex - France

Tel 33 1 49 59 19 72
Fax 33 1 45 21 20 75 
email: geskus at vjf.inserm.fr

--------------------------------------------------------
Answer from Bill Dunlap:

These are bugs.

There are several problems with the function Summary.times() (this is
the function used to compute min, max, and range of times and dates objects).
The first is that its last argument is called drop.na instead of na.rm.
The second is that its default value if T, not F.  The 3rd is that if drop.na
is true it removes the NA's from x but not from the rest of the arguments.
(If it called drop.na na.rm then it wouldn't have to do this removal at
all, since the call to NextMethod would do it for all arguments.)

I believe the enclosed Summary.times will work properly but haven't tested
it much:

"Summary.times"<-
function(x, ..., na.rm = T)
{
        ok <- switch(.Generic,
                max = ,
                min = ,
                range = T,
                FALSE)
        if(!ok)
                stop(paste(.Generic, "not defined for times objects"))
        cl <- class(x)
        fmt <- attr(x, "format")
        if(dates.flg <- inherits(x, "dates"))
                org <- origin(x)
        val <- NextMethod(.Generic)
        attr(val, "format") <- fmt
        if(dates.flg)
                attr(val, "origin") <- org
        class(val) <- cl
        val
}

messages.subject: [S] Multiple frailty terms
messages.body_plain:
The question has come up about multiple frailty terms.  The current code
can be used to do this, with some important restrictions:

   fit <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex +  frailty(family, dist='gauss')
                              + frailty(city, dist='gauss'), data= mydata)
                              
The above doesn't quite work.

     1. The minimization strategy that is used isn't quite smart
enough to handle two frailties at once, and will usually (perhaps
always) get lost.

   One solution to this is to use a profile of fits.  For example
   
   var1 <- seq(from=.05, to=.25, by=.05)
   var2 <- var1
   aicmat <- matrix(length(var1), length(var2))
   for (i in 1:length(var1)) { 
      for(j in 1:length(var2)) {
         fit <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + 
                          frailty(family, dist='gauss', theta=var1[i]) +
                          frailty(city, dist='gauss', theta=var1[i], sparse=F),
                        data=mydata)
        aicmat[i,j] <- 2*diff(fit$loglik) - 2*sum(fit$df)
        }
     }

  2. No more than one of the terms can use the sparse computation trick,
one would normally pick the one with the larger number of levels (since
the speed gain is O(nlevels^2)).  There is a bug in the code here: first
it decides term by term whether "sparse" would help, then later has an
error message for "no more than one sparse term allowed" --- when the
code itself decided to use sparse for both!  The "sparse=F" avoids this
logic flaw.

  3. The formula for multi-term AIC is as above, but I haven't worked out
the gamma frailty/MLE or gaussian/REML formulae for penalized models.
It's on my list of things to do.

    In the above, one would choose the fit with maximal AIC.  Instead of a
fixed set of values, one could use the resultant aic value as the 
maximization target of nlminb() or one of the other Splus general routines.

        Terry Therneau

messages.subject: Re: [S] Summary: stepAIC and glm.control()
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 14 Apr 2000, [iso-8859-1] "Gérald Jean" wrote:

> Thanks to prof. Ripley the solution was simple: just set the iteration limit 
> to
> a higher count on the original model that gets fed into stepAIC.  It works 
> but I
> think it would have been nice to have the same setup as the builtin functions
> step.glm and update, and maybe others, who allow different settings for the
> parameters of glm.control than the ones from the input model.

update alters the way a model is fitted: stepAIC does not. step.glm did
_not_ allow a control parameter when stepAIC was written (nor for some
years afterward), and it does not in 3.4, for example (nor in the White
Book), and that seems a recent MathSoft change contrary to the S
philosophy, as it is only applicable to one method. (StepAIC has much wider
applicability.) In short, there are AFAIK no others, and it is step.glm is
the odd man out, since that is the _purpose_ of update().

Run stepAIC(update(fit, control=...)).  That's the Unix approach: combine
tools, not make every one a kitchen sink (but RMS has a special exception).

[Explanation: Richard M Stallman is the chief author of Emacs, whose icon
was until recently a kitchen sink.]

S has a simple, clean, orthogonal design: that has enormous benefits that
are lost by moving towards the SAS model.  step.glm is highly specific
(and give the wrong answers): stepAIC is a generic solution.

--

messages.subject: [S] Assignment with '=' considered harmful...
messages.body_plain:
Why oh why did Mathsoft introduce '=' as an assignment operator?

Sure, 'x=2' saves one keystroke on 'x<-2', and looks prettier than
'x_2', but I just managed to trash a dataframe thanks to a single
character error.

Create a simple data frame:

> xx_data.frame(x=1:10,y=runif(10))
> xx
    x          y 
 1  1 0.02254344
 2  2 0.48571260
 3  3 0.39027947
 4  4 0.48813299
 5  5 0.63524759
 6  6 0.88648139
 7  7 0.75689625
 8  8 0.82929617
 9  9 0.67684373
10 10 0.51251050

Now look at the row that has x equal to 5.

> xx[xx$x=5,]
  x         y 
5 5 0.6352476

 Yup. But I've mistyped '==' as '='. Hands up anyone who has NEVER done
that? One or two, okay. But anyway, it seems to work, so you may not
even
notice it! But oh dear, look at your data frame now:

> xx
   x          y 
 1 5 0.02254344
 2 5 0.48571260
 3 5 0.39027947
 4 5 0.48813299
 5 5 0.63524759
 6 5 0.88648139
 7 5 0.75689625
 8 5 0.82929617
 9 5 0.67684373
10 5 0.51251050

 crunch.

 You can make the same mistake in C, but compiling with -W gives you a
warning:

eqtest.c:6: warning: suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth
value

 Anyway, I got stung with this today, so I thought I'd vent my annoyance
on the rest
of the world. Can I redefine the '=' operator so it doesn't do
assignments??

Barry Rowlingson
Maths and Stats
Lancaster University
Lancaster UK

messages.subject_clean: [S] Strategy for dealing with data that result in non-proportional hazard
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to analyze continuous data using COXPH. I have tested the
proportional hazards assumption using the method of Grambsch, P. and
Therneau, T as implemented in COX.ZPH. The test indicates that the
proportional hazards assumption is violated. I know that for a categorical
variable violation of the proprtional hazards assumption can often be
addressed by using the STRATA() function when calling COXPH. Is there any
way to address violation of proportionality for a continuous variable?

Thanks

John Sorkin

Program Code:
        print("***FIT1a***")
        fit1a <- coxph(Surv(AGE, STATUS) ~ INS120 +
                BMICC + BMICC^2, data = nona, x = T,  )
        summary(fit1a)
        temp <- cox.zph(fit1a)
        print("Diagnostics for FIT1a")
        print(temp)     # display the results
        plot(temp)      # plot curves
        title("FIT1a")  #

OUTPUT:

[1] "Diagnostics for FIT1a"
                rho     chisq   p
INS120          -0.0299         1.39    2.38e-001
BMICC           0.1699  50.99   9.27e-013
I(BMICC^2)      -0.0792 9.53    2.02e-003
GLOBAL  NA      55.23   6.14e-012

messages.subject: [S] Non-proportional hazards
messages.body_plain:
Note: mail to your return address bounced

There are many ways of dealing with a continuous predictor that
does not behave in proportional hazards, not all of them 
easy.  Here is one simple approximate method: stratify 
on quantiles of the variable and also include the continuous 
variable  in the model (perhaps linear?).
This may take out most of the non-ph, and leaving the
continuous variable in the model will take care of some
lack of fit that occurs when you categorize the continuous
variable.

You might also check whether an accelerated failure time non-ph model fits
a greater proportion of the covariables (e.g., log-logistic, log-normal),
especially if the variables have a short-term effect.  -Frank Harrell

> Therneau, T as implemented in COX.ZPH. The test indicates that the

messages.subject: [S] Principal Components Analysis query
messages.body_plain:
Hi 

This is a statistical question rather than a specific S-Plus problem

I have undertaken a PCA of a data set to quantify the data quality of paper 
records using 4 criteria, and thus hoping to arrive at a final "quality score".

The hope was that PC1 would account for a large fraction of the variance and 
would equate with the overall quality. However, PC1 by itself was only 43% of 
the total variance, with a low loading on 1 of the variables. PC2 then came in 
at 31% with a high loading on this last variable.

The question is whether there is anyway to legitimately combine the 2 
independent PCs into an overall score. Returning to the original data it is 
clear that the sum or average of the 2 PCs does in fact approximate this; 
however, is it nonsence to attempt to combine PCs, and if not should this be 
weighted by the variance proportion or by even a more cleaver method.

Thanks for any advice anyone has on this problem

Peter Durr

Epidemiology
Veterinary Laboraties Agency - Weybridge
New Haw, Addlestone
Surrey
England

messages.subject: [S] workshop announcement
messages.body_plain:
Hello all, I wanted to share with you this announcement for an upcoming
workshop on the analysis of neural data
to be held this summer at woods hole, MA. The workshop has been
extremely productive in the past years and we
anticipate another good working group this year. This workshop is
applicable for any working in time series analysis whether
it involves point processes or sampled continuous time processes. (Both
will be discussed extensively) I am including the
poster for this year's workshop below. I would appreciate it
if you could forward this e-mail to any of your colleagues who might be
interested in these issues. If you have any further questions
I can be reached via e-mail at wmking at bell-labs.com or by phone at (908)

582-2669. Applications should be mailed or faxed to the address listed
in the poster, but I would be happy to answer any of your questions you
might have about the workshop. Please check out the workshop's web site
at www.vis.caltech.edu/~WAND in order to see what has been discussed in
previous years, as well as a list of participants. Thank you for your
attention and help in
disseminating this information.

Sincerely,

Wayne King

Analysis of Neural Data

Modern methods and open issues in the analysis and
interpretation of multivariate time series and imaging data in the
neurosciences

20 August - 2 September 2000

Marine Biological Laboratories - Woods Hole, MA

A working group of scientists committed to quantitative
approaches to problems in neuroscience will focus their
efforts on experimental and theoretical issues related to
the analysis of single and multichannel data sets.

The work group is motivated by issues in two complimentary areas
that are critical to an understanding of brain function. The first
involves advanced signal processing methods, particularly those
appropriate for emerging multisite recording and noninvasive
imaging techniques. The second involves the development of a
calculus to study the dynamical behavior of nervous systems and
the computations they perform.

A distinguishing feature of the work group is a close collaboration
between experimentalists and theorists with regard to the analysis
of data and the planning of experiments. The work group will have
a limited number of research lectures, supplemented by tutorials on
relevant computational, experimental, and mathematical techniques.

The topics covered in the workgroup will maintain continuity with past
years and will include the analysis of point process data (spike trains)
as well as continuous
processes (LFP, imaging data), and miscellaneous topics such as spike
waveform classification. We will have
two one-day workshops in addition to the scheduled activities:

28 August-Neuronal Control Signals for Prosthetic Devices
1 September-Statistical Inference for fMRI Time Series

Participants: About twenty five participants, both experimentalists and
theorists. Experimentalists are encouraged to bring data records to the
work group;
appropriate computational facilities will be provided. The work group
will further take advantage of interested
investigators and course faculty concurrently present at the MBL.

We encourage graduate students and postdoctoral fellows as well as
senior researchers to apply.

PARTICIPANT FEE: $300

Accepted participants will be provided with shared dormitory
accomodations at MBL and board.
Support: National Institutes of Health-NIMH, NIA,  NIAAA, NICHD/NCRR,
NIDCD, NIDA, and NINDS.

Organizers: David Kleinfeld (UCSD) and Partha P. Mitra (Bell
Laboratories, Lucent Technologies).

Website: www.vis.caltech.edu/~WAND/

Application: Send a copy of your c.v. together with a cover letter
that contains a brief (ca. 200 word) paragraph on why you wish to
attend the work group to:

Ms. Jean B. Ainge
Bell Laboratories, Lucent Technologies
700 Mountain Avenue 1D-427
Murray Hill, NJ 07974
908-582-4702 (fax) or <jba at bell-labs.com>

Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows are encouraged to
include a brief letter of support from their research advisor.

Applications must be received by   19 May 2000

Participants will be notified by   29 May 2000

messages.subject: [S] Re: Collinearity Diagnostics
messages.body_plain:
VIF can be calculated easily as follows:

assume lm.obj is your linear regression object

VIF<-diag(solve(cor(model.matrix(lm.obj)[,-1])))

model.matrix extracts the predictor matrix. You want to leave out
column 1 because that is the intercept column.  VIF is the diagonal of
the inverse of the correlation matrix of predictors.

messages.subject: RE: [S] empirical CDF
messages.body_plain:
The empirical CDF should not be diagonal between observed points (unless
you want to interpolate a density), it should be staircase-shaped.
(Hence type="l" does not do quite the right thing.)
The following will do it for you:

delta_diff(range(x))*.05
n_length(x)
plot(c(min(x)-delta,sort(x),max(x)+delta),c(0,0:n/n),type="S")

the "delta" extension at each end is just for looks; of course in principal
the empirical CDF can be extended to plus and minus infinity.  If you 
plot the minimum and maximum, you can see that the steps start and end
in the right place

abline(v=range(x),lty=3)

(Now if you want to be really pedantic you can argue that the vertical 
connecting lines and the last pixel of each horizontal should be deleted,
but that is too damn ugly!)

messages.subject: [S] Scoping rules and Trellis
messages.body_plain:
It is often necessary to assign objects to frame 1 so that they will
be visible to operations on glm objects and the like.  My question is
a variation on that one.

In a Trellis panel function I wish to do some calculations and append
the results to a matrix.  I can do that simply enough like so:

store.mat_NULL
assign("store.mat",store.mat,1)
xxx <- contourplot( blah, blah,   panel = function{
blah, blah,
# Calculate vector in panel
panel.bit <- blah, blah

# append to the matrix
store.mat <- rbind(store.mat, panel.bit)
assign("store.mat",store.mat,1)# so the next panel can see it
}
)
print(xxx)

# Then do something with store.mat

If I put a browser in the panel function, I can see the object
store.mat is being created how I intended it to be done.

However, even though it is assigned to frame 1, it is not visible when
the panel function is finished.  More to the point, it is still the
NULL it was when first created.

Evidently, when the calculations are done during the print(xxx)
section, something different is going on in frame 1 from what I'm
anticipating.

So what *is* really going on, and is there a better way to get the
table without assigning it to and object in the working directory with
immediate = T.  I don't really want an object there.

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: [S] Scoping rules and Trellis
messages.body_plain:
At 02:53 PM 4/20/00 +1200, Patrick Connolly wrote:
>
>It is often necessary to assign objects to frame 1 so that they will
>be visible to operations on glm objects and the like.  My question is
>a variation on that one.
>
>In a Trellis panel function I wish to do some calculations and append
>the results to a matrix.  I can do that simply enough like so
>
>store.mat <- NULL
>assign("store.mat",store.mat,1)
>xxx <- contourplot( blah, blah,   panel = function{
>blah, blah,
># Calculate vector in panel
>panel.bit <- blah, blah
>
># append to the matrix
>store.mat <- rbind(store.mat, panel.bit)
>assign("store.mat",store.mat,1)# so the next panel can see it
>}
>)
>print(xxx)
>
># Then do something with store.mat
>
>If I put a browser in the panel function, I can see the object
>store.mat is being created how I intended it to be done.
>
>However, even though it is assigned to frame 1, it is not visible when
>the panel function is finished.  More to the point, it is still the
>NULL it was when first created.

Recall that frame 1 is born with the expression and dies with the
expression, so as soon as you return to the interactive level frame 1 is
flushed and no longer exists until you initiate another command-line
expression.

>
>Evidently, when the calculations are done during the print(xxx)
>section, something different is going on in frame 1 from what I'm
>anticipating.

Frame 1 is dying sooner than you expect it to die.  If you want some
communication between command line expressions you should (indeed must) put
the result in frame 0 rather than frame 1.  

>
>So what *is* really going on, and is there a better way to get the
>table without assigning it to and object in the working directory with
>immediate = T.  I don't really want an object there.

Use frame 0.  This is created with the session and dies with the session,
so its shelf life is that much longer.

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Sample of Generalised Error Distribution
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Sample of Generalised Error Distribution
messages.body_plain:
The original question was:
 Do you know how one can take sample from a Generalised Error Distribution
 (GED)?

Adelchi Azzalini  <azzalini at stat.unipd.it>
Dipart.Scienze Statistiche, Università di Padova, Italia

Many thanks to Adelchi Azzalini, Dipart.Scienze Statistiche, Università di
Padova, Italia
who provided the following answer:

I presume you are referring to a random variable, X say, with density
function proportional to 
        exp(-|x|^r/r)
where r is positive parameter; so r=2 corresponds to the Normal density.
Then you can you the following function to generate n random numbers from X:

rged <- function(n,r=2) ifelse(runif(n)>0.5,1,-1)*(r*rgamma(n,1/r))^(1/r)

since X can be viewed as 
     X = S (r W)^(1/r) 
where S is a random sign (+1/-1 with equal probability) and W is an
independent Gamma variate of index r.  To compute the density function use
     
dged <- function(x,r=2)  exp(-abs(x)^r/r)/(2*r^(1/r-1)*gamma(1/r))

Spyros.

messages.subject: RE: [S] empirical CDF
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm very happy that there are a lot of responses to my question. Before I
summarize, could someone give an elegant way to plot additional vertical and
horizontal lines corresponding to 25th, 50th and 75th quantitles (or whatever
quantitles you want to look at) on the ecdf graph? Those are the statistics
we usually interested in so I know you know what I mean by vertical and
horizontal
lines.

Best regards,

Jane

zaslavsk at hcp.med.harvard.edu on 19-Apr-2000 16:54

To:   Jane 2 Xu, s-news, sam.martin
cc:
Subject:  RE: [S] empirical CDF

The empirical CDF should not be diagonal between observed points (unless
you want to interpolate a density), it should be staircase-shaped.
(Hence type="l" does not do quite the right thing.)
The following will do it for you:

delta_diff(range(x))*.05
n_length(x)
plot(c(min(x)-delta,sort(x),max(x)+delta),c(0,0:n/n),type="S")

the "delta" extension at each end is just for looks; of course in principal
the empirical CDF can be extended to plus and minus infinity.  If you
plot the minimum and maximum, you can see that the steps start and end
in the right place

abline(v=range(x),lty=3)

(Now if you want to be really pedantic you can argue that the vertical
connecting lines and the last pixel of each horizontal should be deleted,
but that is too damn ugly!)

messages.subject: Re: [S] a trous algorithm for image? (S-News Digest V1 #773)
messages.subject_clean: [S] a trous algorithm for image? (S-News Digest V1 #773)
messages.body_plain:
> Does anyone know if the so-called "a trous" algorithm for redundant >
> wavelet transform for image (matrix data) is implemented in S+?  If > yes,
> where can I find it?  One can find such algorithm in S+Wavelet > module for
> one dimensional signals (vector data)

I wouldn't do this in S-Plus.  It's not optimized for this.  In e.g.

F. Murtagh, J.L. Starck and M. Berry, "Overcoming the curse of 
dimensionality in clustering by means of the wavelet transform",

The Computer Journal, in press, online copy at 
http://www.cs.qub.ac.uk/~F.Murtagh/recent-papers.html

we do noise modeling of around 1000x1000 hypertext array data taken as an 
image.  There is still a lot of mileage in analyzing matrices as images 
(that explains the title of this article!).  S-Plus is really good for some 
things but not for image processing.  (And doing the a trous transform on an 
image of e.g. 100x100 doesn't make much sense - you can certainly code that 
up easily in a couple of lines of S-Plus.)  For dozens of this and other 
wavelet transforms, noise models, applications, etc. see 
http://www.multiresolution.com, for literature and software.

Best regards,
Fionn Murtagh

messages.subject: [S] Summary of responses about empirical CDF
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary of responses about empirical CDF
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Below is a summary of the responses I received regarding plotting Empirical
CDF (and reference quantile lines). I presonally like Alan's ECDF line and
the way Gerrit Eichner plots the quantile lines, so I kinda miss and match and
have my "own" function. Their codes are included below. There are a couple
of people pointed out that Hmisc library in Statlab has this function too. Since
Alan's and Gerrit's codes are good enough for me, I didn't check out the Hmisc
library. Thanks to many more people who also responded.

#################### Alan Zaslavsk's Codes #######################
delta_diff(range(x))*.05
n_length(x)
plot(c(min(x)-delta,sort(x),max(x)+delta),c(0,0:n/n),type="S")
abline(h=0:4/4,lty=3)
abline(v=c(approx(x=(1:length(x)-1)/length(x),y=sort(x),xout=c(.25,.50,.75),
     f=0,method="constant")$y,max(x)),lty=3)

##################### Gerrit Eichner's Function ####################
my.ecdf <- function(x, probs=c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), extfak=0.05, ...) {
     x <- sort(x);                 n <- length(x)
     xext <- (x[n] - x[1])*extfak;       y <- (1:n)/n

     plot(x, y, xlim=c(x[1] - xext, x[n] + xext), ylim=c(0, 1), ...)
     segments(c(x[1] - xext, x), c(0, y), c(x, x[n] + xext), c(0, y))

     abline(h=0:1, lty=2)

     quants <- quantile(x, probs); nq <- length(quants)
     segments(rep(par("usr")[1], nq), probs, quants, probs, lty=3)
     segments(quants, probs, quants, rep(0, nq), lty=3)

     names(quants) <- probs
     invisible(quants)
     }

messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary of responses about empirical CDF
messages.body_plain:
At 09:29 AM 21/4/00 -0400, Jane_2_Xu at sbphrd.com wrote:
>
>Hi All,
>
>Below is a summary of the responses I received regarding plotting Empirical
>CDF (and reference quantile lines). I presonally like Alan's ECDF line and
>the way Gerrit Eichner plots the quantile lines, so I kinda miss and match
and
>have my "own" function. Their codes are included below. ...

Right now I am thinking about teaching again (very briefly!) so I thought this
might make a nice little example of a generic function and a couple of
methods.

The following suite uses essentially the same ideas as in Alan Zaslavsky's
few 
lines of code, but presents it in a slightly more flexible way.  You can call
the function with one sample, several samples (as separate arguments) or a
single
list of samples and it places the ECDFs on the same plot.  The argument q
may be 
used to request quantile lines, e.g. q=1:3/4 asks for the quartiles.  In
addition
given any object inheriting from "lm" results in an ECDF plot of the
residuals.
(Note that statistically normal scores plots are better for looking at
residuals 
ECDF plots, though.)

Note: this is essentially S version 3 OOP.  Converting to S version 4 without
using backward compatibility would require a comprehensive overhaul.

As usual, there are few little tricky bits,  Njoi.  Bill Venables.

---(cut here)---
ecdf <- function(x, ...) {
        if(is.null(class(x)))
                class(x) <- data.class(x)
        UseMethod("ecdf")
}

ecdf.default <- function(x, ..., xlab = "x", q = NULL, ylab = "Empirical
CDF") {
        x <- range(unlist(m <- list(x, ...)), na.rm = T)
        plot(x, 0:1, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, type = "n")
        i <- 0
        pu <- par("usr")
        for(x in m) {
                sx <- sort(as.numeric(x))
                n <- length(x)
                lines(c(pu[1], sx, pu[2]), c(0, 0:n/n), type = "S", 
                        col = i <- i + 1)
                if(!is.null(q)) {
                        qv <- quantile(sx, q)
                        segments(pu[1], q, qv, q, col = i)
                        segments(qv, q, qv, pu[3], col = i)
                }
        }
        invisible(m)
}

ecdf.list <- function(x, ...)
invisible(do.call("ecdf", c(x, list(...))))

ecdf.lm <- function(x, ..., xlab = "Residuals") {
        x <- resid(x)
        invisible(NextMethod("ecdf", x = x, ..., xlab = xlab))
}

messages.subject: Re: [S] Piecewise Linear Regression
messages.body_plain:
Wim Kimmerer asks:

> Hello, I am trying to find an algorithm to do piecewise
> regression when the location of the break is unknown.  I tried
> using nls but I get an error message saying there are N NA's
> (where N is the number of points).  It can be done with bs but
> only if the locations of the knots are known.  There are plenty
> of references to it around but none of them seem to lead to an
> algorithm.  If anybody has a function or suggestion on how to
> do this, I would appreciate hearing about it.
> 
> Wim Kimmerer

Fitting a broken-line regression is not difficult.  For example
if there is only one change of slope (break-point) you could use
three steps:

> fn <- function(th, x, y) { # conditional minimum SSQ given theta
        X <- cbind(x, pmax(0, x - th))
        sum(lsfit(X, y)$resid^2)
}
> th <- optimize(fn, range(x), x = x, y = y)$minimum
> fm <- lm(y ~ x + pmax(0, x - th))

Then th is the break point, and the three regression coefficients
have obvious meanings.

You might be in a spot of bother if you don't even know the
number of break-points and try to estimate it, too.

Even if you know the number of break-points, making any
inferences about the coefficients by any sort of frequentist
methods is a hornet's nest of problems, too, because the
log-likelihood is only piecewise differentiable.  This might be
another one of those cases where "Bayes pays": integrating the
likelihood X prior presents no problem, (in principle).

--

messages.body_plain:
** Reply Requested When Convenient **

Dear Peter,
PCA only works when one had 'good' correlations between the observed variables. 
A good correlation is one between 0.3 and 0.6. Anything more or less will not 
be useful. I bet the last variable is not or weakly correlated with the rest. 
PC1 is usually sum of variables. The others tend to be differences or 
standalones, like the PC2. Any combiantion of the PCs is a combination of the 
original variables. Hence if you combine the PCs, one get backs the original 
variable(s). It defeats the purpose of PCA.
Regards
NJ Sreedharan,
Postgraduate,
Curtin,Perth

>>> "Durr, Peter"  DN=PDURR, RECIPIENTS, CVL, VLA <P.Durr at vla.maff.gsi.gov.uk>

Hi 

This is a statistical question rather than a specific S-Plus problem

I have undertaken a PCA of a data set to quantify the data quality of paper 
records using 4 criteria, and thus hoping to arrive at a final "quality score".

The hope was that PC1 would account for a large fraction of the variance and 
would equate with the overall quality. However, PC1 by itself was only 43% of 
the total variance, with a low loading on 1 of the variables. PC2 then came in 
at 31% with a high loading on this last variable.

The question is whether there is anyway to legitimately combine the 2 
independent PCs into an overall score. Returning to the original data it is 
clear that the sum or average of the 2 PCs does in fact approximate this; 
however, is it nonsence to attempt to combine PCs, and if not should this be 
weighted by the variance proportion or by even a more cleaver method.

Thanks for any advice anyone has on this problem

messages.subject: RE: [S] Piecewise Linear Regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi all:

Bill Venables's modest understatement: 

        "You might be in a spot of bother if you don't even know the number
of break-points and try to estimate it, too. "

As I just finished reading a book on this, I couldn't resist commenting.
This is what the computer science folks call a "machine learning"  problem.
It also may fall in the "Discrete Bayesian Model Uncertainty" paradigm.  In
either case, the idea is that we must not only estimate and do inference on
the parameters of a SINGLE model, but may have to choose the model,too (the
number of break points + parameters for each line segment). Bayesians do
this by putting a (uniform, say) prior on the number of breakpoints which
then leads to a posterior that incorporates uncertainty about the number of
breakpoints, as it should. Machine learning theorists fit a (nested, in this
case) sequence of models and look at measure of prediction accuracy --
usually some form of cross validation, but they've got fancier stuff, too --
to choose the right one.I don't understand how they do inference -- would
someone care to comment further on this?

In either case, the bit about fitting a model when there may be several
breakpoints is nontrivial, (n, k) -- n choose k --  could be large. However,
if the data sets are not very big and k is small, then since the fits
(conditional on the location of the breakpoints) are linear it shouldn't be
much of a problem even with cross validation.

This is a good example of how an apparently straightforward issue -- how to
fit and do inference for piecewise simple linear regression -- leads to
complications. S-Plus's flexibility is very nice to have here. 

Of course, ignore all this if what you really want is what Bill said -- a
SINGLE breakpoint.

Cheers,

messages.subject: [S] Piecewise Linear Regression
messages.body_plain:
It is also possible to fit a linear break point model where the break
point is a true parameter in the model The model function below will
work in nls.  It includes a very short quadratic piece where the break
point is to keep the derivative w.r.t. the break point continuous.  -
Mary Lindstrom

hockey <- function(x,alpha1,beta1,beta2,brk,eps=range(x)/100) {
       ## alpha1 is the intercept of the left line segment
       ## beta1 is the slope of the left line segment
       ## beta2 is the slope of the right line segment
       ## brk is location of the break point
       ## 2*eps is the length of the connecting quadratic piece

       ## reference: Bacon & Watts "Estimating the Transition Between
       ## Two Intersecting Straight Lines", Biometrika, 1971

        x1 _ brk-eps
        x2 _ brk+eps
        b <- (x2*beta1-x1*beta2)/(x2-x1)
        cc <- (beta2-b)/(2*x2)
        a <- alpha1+beta1*x1-b*x1-cc*x1^2
        alpha2 _ - beta2*x2 +(a + b*x2 + cc*x2^2)

        lebrk <- (x <= brk-eps)
        gebrk <- (x >= brk+eps)
        eqbrk <- (x > brk-eps & x < brk+eps)

        result <- rep(0,length(x))
        result[lebrk] <- alpha1 + beta1*x[lebrk]
        result[eqbrk] <- a + b*x[eqbrk] + cc*x[eqbrk]^2
        result[gebrk] <- alpha2 + beta2*x[gebrk]
        result
}

 > Hello, I am trying to find an algorithm to do piecewise regression when the

survreg) that includes a frailty term, and I want to get a p-value for that
factor.

fit1<-coxph(Surv(time,censor)~other.stuff+factorA+gamma.frailty(id))
fit2<-coxph(Surv(time,censor)~other.stuff+gamma.frailty(id))

1-pchisq(-2*(fit2$loglik[2]-fit1$loglik[2]),df=sum(fit1$df)-sum(fit2$df))

of factorA -1), because fit1 and fit2 have different df's also because the
df from the frailty term differ. And occasionally this does
make a difference (say, the factor has only three levels, but the df's change
due to the frialty is of 4). I think that the correct approach is to use, as df,
the number of levels of the excluded factor minus 1.

messages.subject: Re: [S] tapply with a exclusionary index
messages.body_plain:
At 04:50 PM 4/24/00 -0400, Martin H. H. Stevens wrote:
>
>
>How do I do a tapply where the index is based on a ?not? statement
>(e.g., !=)
>
>For instance:
>
>Index <- c(a,a,a,b,b,b,c,c,c)
>Response <- c(1,2,3,4,5,6,2,4,7)
>
>I would like to calculate the mean Response 3 times, each time excluding
>one of the levels of Index.  I thought it might look something like:
>
>means.minus.each.level <- tapply(Response, !=Index, mean)
>
>but this (and its variants) didn?t work, so?.any ideas?

(Well, a syntax error is a pretty good indication it's not going to work...)

Think of tapply() working in two stages:

1. split the vector into *discrete* (non-intersecting) groups first.

2. present each group, in turn, to the function.

Your problem is that you want to split the vector into *non*-discrete,
*intersecting* groups, so you have to work indirectly and present the
function with an index of what to leave out, rather than the bit to use.

Here is one way to do it.

> Index
[1] "a" "a" "a" "b" "b" "b" "c" "c" "c"
> Response
[1] 1 2 3 4 5 6 2 4 7
> tapply(seq(along = Response), Index, 
             function(i) mean(Response[-i]))
      a      b         c 
 4.6667 3.1667 3.5

This relies on Response being globally visible, so it may not work if you
try to do it inside a function.

Minor tip:  for simple uses of tapply() it is often quicker to make do with
lower level tools such as

        unlist(lapply(split(vector, index), func))

for example:

> unlist(lapply(split(seq(along = Response), Index), 
                function(i) mean(Response[-i])))
      a      b   c 
 4.6667 3.1667 3.5

Bill Venables.

messages.body_plain:
At 09:10 AM 4/24/00 -0500, Mary Lindstrom wrote:
>
>It is also possible to fit a linear break point model where the break
>point is a true parameter in the model The model function below will
>work in nls.  It includes a very short quadratic piece where the break
>point is to keep the derivative w.r.t. the break point continuous.  -
>Mary Lindstrom
>
>hockey <- function(x,alpha1,beta1,beta2,brk,eps=range(x)/100) {

Hmm.  I think that should be  eps = diff(range(x))/100

>       ## alpha1 is the intercept of the left line segment
>       ## beta1 is the slope of the left line segment
>       ## beta2 is the slope of the right line segment
>       ## brk is location of the break point
>       ## 2*eps is the length of the connecting quadratic piece
>
>       ## reference: Bacon & Watts "Estimating the Transition Between
>       ## Two Intersecting Straight Lines", Biometrika, 1971
>
>        x1 _ brk-eps
>        x2 _ brk+eps
>        b <- (x2*beta1-x1*beta2)/(x2-x1)
>        cc <- (beta2-b)/(2*x2)
>        a <- alpha1+beta1*x1-b*x1-cc*x1^2
>        alpha2 _ - beta2*x2 +(a + b*x2 + cc*x2^2)
>
>        lebrk <- (x <= brk-eps)
>        gebrk <- (x >= brk+eps)
>        eqbrk <- (x > brk-eps & x < brk+eps)
>
>        result <- rep(0,length(x))
>        result[lebrk] <- alpha1 + beta1*x[lebrk]
>        result[eqbrk] <- a + b*x[eqbrk] + cc*x[eqbrk]^2
>        result[gebrk] <- alpha2 + beta2*x[gebrk]
>        result
>}

With this one change it works pretty well in nls for me.  

Another advantage of doing it this way is that you can inspect the
log-likelihood through profile and pairs.profile plots.  If they look OK
you can get reasonable confidence intervals without the help of brother
Bayes after all.  For the example I took both plots seemed utterly tame.

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: [S] Summary : How can I remove this loop !!!
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary : How can I remove this loop !!!
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

thanks for all the answers I have received ...

My problem was :

> I have 2 lists (named list1 and list2) with the same
> length (or one list (list1) and a vector (named vect)
> which have the same length).
> I would like to make some operations betwenn the
> two's component by component without loop:
>
> example:
> for (i in 1:length(list1)){
>         A[[i]]<-list1[[i]]/vect[i]
> }
> (or A[[i]]<-list1[[i]]%*%list2[[i]])

Here are the 2 solutions (very closed) that I prefer :

1) from Bill Dunlap :

     A <- lapply(seq(along=list1),
             function(i, numerator, denominator)
     numerator[[i]/denominator[i],
             numerator=list1, denominator=vect)
     A <- lapply(seq(along=list1),
             function(i, x, y) x[[i]] %*% y[[i]],
             x, y)

although it may not save a lot of time to do it that way.  (The simpler
the function you are iterating, the bigger the gain you get from
lapply.)

2) from  Andreas Krause

        A <- lapply(as.list(1:length(list1)), function(i, l, v)
     l[[i]]/v[[i]], l=list1, v=list2)

      --------- myrtille.

messages.subject: [Fwd: [S] dotplot on a log scale
messages.body_plain:
To produce a dot plot using a log scale and get a pre-determined
number of labeled tick marks (say 4) to appear on the x-axis, the following
seems to do the trick:

dotplot(Group ~ Xvalue | ConditioningVar,
subset=(Xvalue>0),
scale = list(x = list(log = T,
at = pretty(log(Xvalue[Xvalue > 0],base=10), nint = 5)),
labels=10^pretty(log(Xvalue[Xvalue > 0],base=10), nint = 5))))

Note that "pretty" does not guarantee 'nint' intervals.
We need to use the "pretty" function for automating the process.

Thanks to Bill Venables and Marcel Baumgartner for suggesting the solution.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Scoping rules and Trellis
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Bill Venables for his help.

I had tried assigning my object to frame 0 but it was not available
until the function had exited.  That wasn't good enough.  However once
at Bill's suggestion I used get to retrieve it specifically from frame
0, all was well.

For anyone who has a similar problem, the solution is to change this
line:

assign("store.mat",store.mat,1)

to 
assign("store.mat",store.mat,0)

Then, to make use of store.mat, 

store.mat<- get("store.mat",frame=0)

Were we using a glm, assigning to frame 1 would have made the object
available simply by naming it any time while the expression is
running.  When the assigning is done within a panel function, the
frame 1 changes die when the panel function is exited.

I don't understand why get needs to be used specifically, but this
seems to be how the rules work, even if I can't explain the thinking
behind them.

As ever, thanks again to Bill Venables.

The question I asked was this:

It is often necessary to assign objects to frame 1 so that they will
be visible to operations on glm objects and the like.  My question is
a variation on that one.

In a Trellis panel function I wish to do some calculations and append
the results to a matrix.  I can do that simply enough like so:

store.mat_NULL
assign("store.mat",store.mat,1)
xxx <- contourplot( blah, blah,   panel = function{
blah, blah,
# Calculate vector in panel
panel.bit <- blah, blah

# append to the matrix
store.mat <- rbind(store.mat, panel.bit)
assign("store.mat",store.mat,1)# so the next panel can see it
}
)
print(xxx)

# Then do something with store.mat

If I put a browser in the panel function, I can see the object
store.mat is being created how I intended it to be done.

However, even though it is assigned to frame 1, it is not visible when
the panel function is finished.  More to the point, it is still the
NULL it was when first created.

Evidently, when the calculations are done during the print(xxx)
section, something different is going on in frame 1 from what I'm
anticipating.

So what *is* really going on, and is there a better way to get the
table without assigning it to and object in the working directory with
immediate = T.  I don't really want an object there.

Thanks

--

Patrick Connolly
HortResearch
Mt Albert
Auckland
New Zealand 
Ph: +64-9 815 4200 x 7188

>>From the online manual (I never use it but..):

DESCRIPTION Tests for existence of directories with given names.

USAGE
   is.dir(dir)

REQUIRED ARGUMENTS
  dir   a character vector of possible directory names.

VALUE
 a logical vector the length of the input containing TRUE for each input
name that is a directory.  There is also an attribute called error
containing a short description of why a name is not a directory.

SEE ALSO

file.exists, mkdir, rmdir.

EXAMPLES

if (file.exists("xyz") && !is.dir("xyz"))

cat("xyz is a file but not a directory\n")
